power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: To test whether the non-significant simple effects indicate the absence of a difference, we conducted TOST equivalence tests (not preregistered). For each effect, the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) was set to the bound at which the TOST procedure has 80% power at α = .05 when the true effect is zero, given that effect's empirical SE. In the actual advice condition, the influence of AI and human advice was statistically equivalent: we can reject source differences larger than 0.048 WOA units, t(1881) = -1.82, p = .034. For AI advice, the influence expected in the hypothetical condition was equivalent to the influence observed in the actual condition at the group level: we can reject mode differences larger than 0.066, t(625) = -1.84, p = .033. For human advice, the test was inconclusive (SESOI = 0.066, t(636) = 1.42, p = .077): expected influence was somewhat higher than actual influence, but this difference was neither significant nor demonstrably absent. Taken together, participants expected less influence from AI than from human advice, whereas both sources were equally influential when advice was actually received.
table.header: Preregistered Analysis

table.text: 401 participants completed the survey on prolific.com. Inclusion criteria were being a native English speaker, having an approval rate of at least 95% of previous surveys on the platform, and not having participated in previous studies using similar material. Target sample size (N = 400) was determined by a power simulation based on pilot data (see OSF repository for code). In a linear model predicting weight of advice from advice mode, advice source, and their interaction, this sample size should yield over 80% power to detect a positive interaction coefficient of 𝛽 = 0.07 (as underestimating weight of advice more for AI than for humans would be indicated by a significant interaction effect in this design). Participants were paid ￡1.20 for an estimated 8 minutes of their time (￡9/hour). 11 Participants were excluded for failing the Müller-Lyer illusion, leaving a final sample size of 390 valid responses (mean age = 42.52 years, SD = 12.97 years, 192 female, 192 male, 1 non-binary, 1 another gender, 2 prefer not to say, 2 missing). Of the 384 participants with available ethnicity data, the majority identified as White (273), followed by Black (69), Asian (25), Mixed (12), and Other (5). Of the 388 participants with available residence data, most resided in the United Kingdom (232) or the United States (82), followed by Canada (24), South Africa (22), Australia (13), and Ireland (8); 7 resided in other countries.

You reported a power analysis that has been classified as 'post-hoc'. Calculating observed power is [almost never useful](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/08-samplesizejustification.html#sec-posthocpower). If you actually performed a sensitivity power analysis, label it as such explicitly.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: moral advisors - advice elicitation study
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions: Participants read a set of realistic moral scenarios and are asked to write persuasive advice either in favor of or against the acceptability of the focal action (e.g., staying silent when witnessing inappropriate behavior). They are instructed to produce high-quality, convincing advice directed at future participants (financially incentivized for persuasiveness). After writing each advice paragraph, participants rate (a) the degree to which their advice conveys that the action is morally acceptable, and (b) how morally acceptable they personally find the action, both on 0–100 scales (0 = not acceptable at all, 100 = fully acceptable). Each participant completes multiple randomly selected scenarios from a larger pool. The goal is to collect human-generated advice texts, along with perceived message content and personal acceptability ratings, to construct stimuli for an experimental study. There is no confirmatory hypothesis to be tested in this pre-study, but we may conduct a series of exploratory analyses to characterize the collected stimuli and to compare human-generated advice to advice generated by the Large Language Model GPT-4o.
table.design_dependent_variables:
1) Advice text: For each scenario, participants write a persuasive paragraph arguing that the focal action is either acceptable or not acceptable.
2) Conveyed acceptability: After writing the advice, participants rate how acceptable the action is according to the content of the advice they have just written (0 = not acceptable at all; 100 = fully acceptable).
3) Personal acceptability: Participants also rate how acceptable they personally find the action (0–100 scale with the same anchors).
table.study_design_overview:
Each participant is randomly assigned, for each scenario, to one of two instruction conditions:
1) Argue that the action is acceptable
2) Argue that the action is not acceptable
This assignment is done at the trial level, meaning the same participant may write advice in favor of the action for some scenarios and against it for others. The scenario set is randomized across participants from a larger pool. There are no between-subject conditions.
table.statistical_tests:
The primary purpose of this pre-study is to generate a diverse pool of human-written advice texts, accompanied by acceptability ratings. No confirmatory analyses are planned.

We may conduct the following optional exploratory analyses to better understand the structure and content of the collected advice texts (and compare the results to analyses of similar LLM-generated advice texts):

- Text length (e.g., word or character count)
- Sentiment analysis to classify advice as positive, negative, or neutral
- LLM-assisted coding of moral argument components (e.g., harm, fairness, consequences)
- Semantic embedding and clustering
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
Individual responses will be excluded if they:
- Contain no substantive advice (e.g., filler, nonsensical, or off-topic text)
- Contain personal identifying information (e.g., names, contact info)
- Contain content that would be inappropriate or potentially harmful to show to other participants (e.g., graphic violence, hate speech, slurs, or threats)

Participants will be fully excluded if they:
- Fail the instruction check, which asks: "Which of the following is TRUE about this study?" with the correct answer being: "You will write both pro and contra moral advice, depending on the assigned instruction." They are given two attempts to answer correctly.
- Fail either of two verbal attention checks: 1) Implausible statement (e.g., "I have never taken a survey before, including this one") → Correct response: Disagree or Strongly disagree, 2) Directed-response item instructing participants to select "Disagree" regardless of content → Any other response indicates inattention
- Submit AI-generated or AI-assisted advice texts, as flagged by GPTZero: All advice texts written by a participant will be pasted together and analyzed as a batch. If GPTZero classifies the output as AI-generated or Human–AI co-created, the participant will be excluded.
- Fail a modified Müller-Lyer illusion test in which the two lines are clearly not equally long (the blue line is indeed clearly longer). Participants will be excluded if they give any other answer than "blue" to the question "Which line is longer?".

table.research_questions: Do people underestimate how much they are influenced by AI moral advice?
table.design_dependent_variables:
WOA (weight of advice). 

In the actual advice condition, WOA is computed as: (judgment_revised - judgment_initial) / (advice - judgment_initial). For the main analysis, we will exclude values that are NA (occurs when initial judgment and advice are identical), and values below 0 or above 1 to ensure comparability across conditions.

In the hypothetical advice condition, WOA is assessed by asking: "To what extent could advice from (a Large Language Model (e.g., ChatGPT)/a previous study participant) change your opinion about this situation?", scale ranging from 0 (not at all) to 100 (fully), rescaled to range between 0 and 1 for main analysis.
table.study_design_overview:
2 × 2 mixed design: participants are assigned between-subjects to an advice mode (hypothetical vs. actual) and complete six trials where the within-subjects advice source varies (AI vs. human, randomly drawn at the trial level). Scenarios are drawn from a list of 24 cases (treated as random effect in the analysis). 

In the "actual advice" condition, each trial presents a scenario and elicits an initial moral judgment about the scenario (how acceptable is the target action, rated on a scale ranging from 0, completely unacceptable at all, to 100, completely acceptable). Then, an advice text plus the advisor's numerical acceptability score is presented (human or AI). Finally, participants provide a second moral judgment about the scenario. In the hypothetical condition, participants also read the initial scenario and provide an initial moral judgment. Then they rate how much they think that AI moral advice or human moral advice could change their opinion about this scenario.
table.statistical_tests:
Factors use treatment coding with levels ordered condition = c("hypothetical","actual") and source = c("human","ai"), so the baseline is hypothetical_human.

We compute:

m0 <- lmer(WOA ~ condition + source + (1|id) + (1|scenario), data = dat)
m1 <- lmer(WOA ~ condition * source + (1|id) + (1|scenario), data = dat)

anova(m0, m1) 

The hypothesis is confirmed if adding the interaction improves model fit as indicated by the likelihood ratio test (alpha <= 0.05) AND if the interaction coefficient is positive (conditionactual:sourceai > 0), indicating that the actual–hypothetical gap is larger for AI moral advice than for human moral advice).

We follow up with simple effects to further characterize the difference between actual and hypothetical weight of advice for both human and ai moral advice: 

emm <- emmeans(m1, ~ condition | source)
contrast(emm, method = "revpairwise", adjust = "none")
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
Individual WOA scores from the "actual" condition will be excluded when they are NA (occurs when initial judgment and advice are identical), and if below 0 or above 1, to enable comparability across conditions.

Participants will be excluded if they fail two simple attention checks (screened out live during survey):
1) Which of these is not an animal? Please select "Elephant". (Response options: Dog, Cat, Elephant, Chair). Correct response: Elephant.
2) Please indicate how much you agree or disagree with the following claim: I can hold my breath underwater for five hours without any equipment. (Response options: Strongly disagree, disagree, agree, strongly agree). Correct responses: Strongly disagree, disagree.

Furthermore, participants will be excluded if they fail a bot check in the form of a fake optical illusion (designed to screen out LLM-generated responses). They will see a modified version of the Müller-Lyer illusion in which the top line with outward-pointing arrows is clearly longer than the bottom line with inward-pointing arrows. They will be asked which line is longer (response options: blue (top line), red (bottom line), they are equally long. The correct response option is "blue (top line)", those who respond differently will be excluded from analyses.
table.sample_size: We will recruit 400 participants on prolific.com, inclusion criteria: native English speakers, approval rate of previous submissions at least 95%, not having participated in previous studies related to this project, e.g., pilots and the advice elicitation task. Based on a power simulation using pilot data, the minimal effect size of the interaction that we can detect with sufficient power (81.5%) with this sample size is beta = 0.07.
table.additional_comments:
Human and AI moral advice (elicited in a separate study and consisting of a text paragraph paired with an acceptability score) is filtered in the following way before being included in the design of this current study: If advisors were prompted to write pro advice for that scenario (argue that the action is acceptable), acceptability scores should be at least 50, inclusive (scale: 0, not acceptable at all, to 100, fully acceptable). If prompted to write negative advice, acceptability scores should be below 50.

After completion of the main study, participants fill in the "attitudes towards AI" scale developed by Stein et al., 2024 (Stein, JP., Messingschlager, T., Gnambs, T. et al. Attitudes towards AI: measurement and associations with personality. Sci Rep 14, 2909 (2024). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-53335-2).

Exploratory analyses may examine individual differences and content-level predictors of advice uptake. We might test whether participants with more positive attitudes toward AI show less underestimation of its influence, and whether WOA for AI advisors correlates with demographic variables such as age, gender, or education. For human advisors, we may explore whether their advice is more effective when it aligns with their own moral beliefs, or when it aligns with the participant's initial moral judgment. We might also examine whether AI and human advisors differ in their effectiveness depending on whether the advice supports or challenges the advisee's initial stance. Additionally, we may compare the content of human and AI moral advice and explore which textual features (e.g., length, tone, or argument type) correlate with WOA.

stat_check.title: StatCheck
stat_check.summary_text: 3 possible errors in t-tests or F-tests

table.text: Neither was significant on its own: for AI advice, actual WOA was slightly higher than hypothetical WOA (b = 0.025, SE = 0.023, t(633) = 1.08, p = .280); for human advice, actual WOA was slightly lower than hypothetical WOA (b = -0.034, SE = 0.023, t(644) = -1.50, p = .134).
table.header: Preregistered Analysis

table.text: Neither was significant on its own: for AI advice, actual WOA was slightly higher than hypothetical WOA (b = 0.025, SE = 0.023, t(633) = 1.08, p = .280); for human advice, actual WOA was slightly lower than hypothetical WOA (b = -0.034, SE = 0.023, t(644) = -1.50, p = .134).
table.header: Preregistered Analysis

table.text: Decomposing the interaction the other way (not preregistered) showed that the source difference was located in expectations: participants in the hypothetical condition rated AI advice as less influential than human advice (b = -0.040, SE = 0.016, t(1835) = -2.57, p = .010), whereas in the actual condition, AI and human advice did not differ in influence (b = 0.018, SE = 0.016, t(1884) = 1.10, p = .270).
table.header: Preregistered Analysis

table.text: Decomposing the interaction the other way (not preregistered) showed that the source difference was located in expectations: participants in the hypothetical condition rated AI advice as less influential than human advice (b = -0.040, SE = 0.016, t(1835) = -2.57, p = .010), whereas in the actual condition, AI and human advice did not differ in influence (b = 0.018, SE = 0.016, t(1884) = 1.10, p = .270).
table.header: Preregistered Analysis

table.text: In the actual advice condition, the influence of AI and human advice was statistically equivalent: we can reject source differences larger than 0.048 WOA units, t(1881) = -1.82, p = .034.
table.header: Preregistered Analysis

table.text: For AI advice, the influence expected in the hypothetical condition was equivalent to the influence observed in the actual condition at the group level: we can reject mode differences larger than 0.066, t(625) = -1.84, p = .033.
table.header: Preregistered Analysis

table.text: For human advice, the test was inconclusive (SESOI = 0.066, t(636) = 1.42, p = .077): expected influence was somewhat higher than actual influence, but this difference was neither significant nor demonstrably absent.
table.header: Preregistered Analysis

table.text: Extremity significantly improved fit over source alone (χ²(1) = 5.32, p = .021) and independently predicted somewhat greater uptake (b extremity = 0.0018, SE = 0.0008, 95% CI [0.0003, 0.0034], t(911) = 2.31, p = .021).
table.header: Convergence of Actual and Hypothetical WOA:

table.text: Furthermore, once extremity was controlled, the source effect became significant (b AI = 0.044, SE = 0.021, 95% CI [0.002, 0.085], t(900) = 2.08, p = .038).
table.header: Convergence of Actual and Hypothetical WOA:

table.text: Accordingly, change scores were best described by a linear model containing only a fixed effect of advice direction (b pro = 16.64, SE = 0.95, 95% CI [14.78, 18.50], t(1236.32) = 17.53, p < .001), in addition to random intercepts for participant and scenario.
table.formatted: Accordingly, change scores were best described by a linear model containing only a fixed effect of advice direction (b pro = 16.64, SE = 0.95, 95% CI [14.78, 18.50], t(1236.32) = 17.53, p < .001), in addition to random intercepts for participant and scenario.
table.header: Convergence of Actual and Hypothetical WOA:

table.text: A larger gap will yield a larger raw shift under equal proportional uptake, and WOA itself indeed did not differ by direction (M pro = 0.28, SD = 0.32; M contra = 0.26, SD = 0.32; b pro = 0.005, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [-0.03, 0.04], t(902.7) = 0.28, p = .779, in a linear model predicting WOA from direction with random intercepts for participant and scenario).

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "ps >= .07", Text = "Two features significantly predicted WOA: Flesch-Kincaid grade level, and average sentence length; none of the remaining eight reached significance (all other ps >= .07)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. stat_effect_size.summary_text: We found 7 t-tests and/or F-tests where effect sizes are not reported. Check these tests in the table below, and consider adding effect sizes.

table.text: Neither was significant on its own: for AI advice, actual WOA was slightly higher than hypothetical WOA (b = 0.025, SE = 0.023, t(633) = 1.08, p = .280); for human advice, actual WOA was slightly lower than hypothetical WOA (b = -0.034, SE = 0.023, t(644) = -1.50, p = .134).
table.d_coherence_note: No parseable d effect size found.

table.text: Neither was significant on its own: for AI advice, actual WOA was slightly higher than hypothetical WOA (b = 0.025, SE = 0.023, t(633) = 1.08, p = .280); for human advice, actual WOA was slightly lower than hypothetical WOA (b = -0.034, SE = 0.023, t(644) = -1.50, p = .134).
table.d_coherence_note: No parseable d effect size found.

table.text: Decomposing the interaction the other way (not preregistered) showed that the source difference was located in expectations: participants in the hypothetical condition rated AI advice as less influential than human advice (b = -0.040, SE = 0.016, t(1835) = -2.57, p = .010), whereas in the actual condition, AI and human advice did not differ in influence (b = 0.018, SE = 0.016, t(1884) = 1.10, p = .270).
table.d_coherence_note: No parseable d effect size found.

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 30 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: editor settings (12), Jupyter checkpoints (12), operating system (4), R history (2). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

-  We classified 680 files: 189 data, 346 code, 105 documentation, 38 materials, 2 unknown.
-  We found 109 tabular data files and extracted 66 columns from 3 of them.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 66 columns across 3 data files.
#### Issues Identified

3 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 3 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: This set of two studies received ethical approval from the Institutional Review Board of [blinded for peer review], approval number LIP-2024-08, prior to data collection.
live_data_statements: Participants were equally influenced by human and AI moral advice, revising their judgments by a little under a third of the distance to the advice.

In a foundational series of (pre-GPT) studies, Bigman and Gray (2018) found that participants were reluctant to let machines make morally consequential decisions in areas such as medicine, law, warfare, and autonomous driving, a pattern they linked in part to the perception that machines lack the kind of "mind" needed for legitimate moral judgment.
Although participants were often indifferent or somewhat averse to algorithmic advice in hypothetical reports, they relied on it as much as or more than human advice in actual judgment tasks.
In a second study, a new sample of participants completed a Judge-Advisor System task using a subset of these scenarios.
All participants provided informed consent before participation.

For each scenario, participants were randomly assigned to write advice either pro or contra an action that the agent in the scenario was considering ("Write persuasive advice explaining why it is [not] acceptable for Maya to say no to lending Rachel the money").

This task was incentivized: Participants were informed that their writing would be used in a future advice-taking study, and that they could earn a bonus of 3 if one of their pieces of advice would be among the top 10 percent of the most convincing pieces of advice.
Participants had to correctly answer an instruction check within two attempts before starting the main task ("Which of the following is TRUE about this study?"

After completing the survey, we asked again whether they had used any AI tools (and if so, for what), emphasizing that this would not affect the approval of their submission on prolific.com, but merely inform our interpretation of the data.
101 participants completed the survey on prolific.com.
Participants had to be native English speakers, have an approval rate of previous studies on the platform of at least 95%, and not have participated in previous studies using the same materials.
Participants were paid ￡3 for an estimated 15 minutes of their time (￡12/hour).
Seven participants were excluded for failing the first attention check, one for failing the Müller-Lyer bot check, and one because their text was flagged as AI-generated by gptzero.me.
Participants were randomly assigned to either the actual or the hypothetical advice condition.
The six scenarios shown to one participant were randomly drawn from the full set of 24 scenarios, without replacement.

"Advice from AI (GPT-4)"), and the numerical acceptability score was presented below the advice, visualized as a selected value on a sliding scale like the one participants had used on the previous page.
After reading the advice and continuing to the next page, participants were asked for a second moral judgment of the case ("Please evaluate the scenario once more").

Instead, participants were simply asked: "To what extent could advice from previous study participants [a Large Language Model (e.g., ChatGPT)] change your opinion about this situation?", rated on a numbered sliding scale ranging from 0 ("not at all") to 100 ("fully").

After completing all six scenarios, participants completed a 12-item "Attitudes towards AI" survey (Stein et al., 2024) before the experiment ended with a debriefing and the assessment of demographic variables.
401 participants completed the survey on prolific.com.
Participants were paid ￡1.20 for an estimated 8 minutes of their time (￡9/hour).

11 Participants were excluded for failing the Müller-Lyer illusion, leaving a final sample size of 390 valid responses (mean age = 42.52 years, SD = 12.97 years, 192 female, 192 male, 1 non-binary, 1 another gender, 2 prefer not to say, 2 missing).
Thus, across advisor types, participants were somewhat more persuaded by linguistically more complex advice.
How semantically typical or unusual an advice text is, whether at the level of the individual text or the advisor group, appears to be orthogonal to how much participants are persuaded by it.

In the actual advice condition of our study, participants were equally influenced by human and AI advice, revising their moral judgments by just under 30% of the distance between their initial position and the advice score, regardless of source (27% for humans, 28% for AI).

In addition, since each piece of advice consisted of a written paragraph together with a numerical acceptability score, we cannot say which component did the work, i.e., whether participants were persuaded by the text or were simply anchoring on the number.
Second, our participants did not choose to receive moral advice: they were simply presented with it.

**3 scripts failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. **`setwd()` in the code**

**1 script calls `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.
Reproducible after removing `setwd()`: 06_text_analyses_mfd.Rmd.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "06_text_analyses_mfd.Rmd", "setwd() removed" = 1L, 
    "Path(s) it set" = "(non-literal)"), row.names = c(NA, -1L
), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```

**1 script uses functions from packages it does not load itself.** The packages are usually loaded in another script of the project, which only helps when the scripts run in one R session in the right order. **`os.chdir()` in the code**

**1 script calls `os.chdir()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with `pass`. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring an `os.chdir()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

#### Reported vs. reproduced
106 statistical tests reported in the manuscript text were checked against the extracted analysis output: 6 matched (5 fully, 1 partially) — 5.7% found.

Some reported values were only found alongside OTHER components after being separated from their own originally-reported neighbours (e.g. a mean split from its own confidence interval). The "Plausible" column marks whether that split is well-supported: TRUE when the pieces still trace back to the same underlying variable (via the output's own row labels), FALSE when no such link was found — a FALSE match is not necessarily wrong, but is worth checking against its own Source file/Analysis columns before treating it as confirmed.
#### Self-reproducible output (JASP / jamovi / SPSS Viewer / Jupyter notebook)

1 JASP/jamovi/SPSS-Viewer/notebook file bundles the analyses and their saved results together, so the reported statistics are recoverable from the file itself, with nothing re-run. We extracted 24 result tables (405 individual statistics), typed with the STATO ontology, and export them as a statistical-output JSON document (in the logs) and as queryable rows.

text.text: People are often skeptical of AI in the moral domain, yet AI-generated ethical advice can influence moral judgments as much as human advice.

Unlike most prior work, which attaches human or AI labels to identical advice, we examined how much real advice written by humans and by AI influences moral judgments, and whether people expect less influence from AI than from human advice.
First, we developed 24 realistic everyday moral scenarios and collected over 500 persuasive advice texts from both incentivized human writers (N = 92) and GPT-4o.
AI-generated advice was longer, more linguistically complex, more semantically uniform, more virtue-oriented, and less extreme than human advice.
Next, a new sample of participants (N = 390) either revised initial moral judgments after receiving human or AI advice or indicated how much they expected such advice to influence them.
Participants were equally influenced by human and AI moral advice, revising their judgments by a little under a third of the distance to the advice.
Participants who only estimated the influence, however, expected less influence from AI than from human advice.
These findings suggest that skepticism toward AI in moral contexts may shape people's expectations about AI moral advice, but not how much they are actually influenced by it.
During the preparation of this work the authors used generative AI (Large Language Models like Claude and GPT) to refine the phrasing of pre-drafted text passages and to shorten text passages.
LLM assistance was also partially used in coding and in creating supplementary files (e.g., READMEs).
The authors reviewed and edited the content as needed and take full responsibility for the content of the published article.
AI systems are increasingly embedded in contexts that involve recommendation, evaluation, and guidance.

Both provider reports and emerging academic research indicate that people use Large Language Models (LLMs) not only for information retrieval and task completion, but also for practical advice and interpersonal support, including coaching, counseling, and related personal concerns (Anthropic, 2025; Chatterji et al., 2025; Manoli et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Both provider reports and emerging academic research indicate that people use Large Language Models (LLMs) not only for information retrieval and task completion, but also for practical advice and interpersonal support, including coaching, counseling, and related personal concerns <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Anthropic, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Chatterji et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Manoli et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Zheng et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Even when users do not explicitly ask for advice about right and wrong, AI systems can still express values (Hadar-Shoval et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Even when users do not explicitly ask for advice about right and wrong, AI systems can still express values <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Hadar-Shoval et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Huang et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In recommending actions, weighing considerations, or explaining why one option is better than another, they often convey implicit views about what is fair, acceptable, harmful, or worth prioritizing.
This means that exposure to morally relevant AI output may arise not only through deliberate advice-seeking, but also through routine use of these systems for more general guidance.

Thus, AI systems are increasingly encroaching into a sphere that was for the longest time considered to be uniquely and distinctively human, central for both personal (Strohminger & Nichols, 2014) and collective identity (Ayala, 2010).
text.formatted: Thus, AI systems are increasingly encroaching into a sphere that was for the longest time considered to be uniquely and distinctively human, central for both personal <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Strohminger & Nichols, 2014)</ref> and collective identity <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Ayala, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The growing presence of AI in morally relevant forms of guidance raises a natural question: how comfortable are people with artificial systems taking on this role?

After all, even if the use of AI for ethical guidance is becoming more common, those who actively turn to such systems for moral advice may still constitute only a small subset of the population, and their behavior may diverge from more general public opinion.
Psychological research probing stated opinions and attitudes suggests that this could be the case.

In a foundational series of (pre-GPT) studies, Bigman and Gray (2018) found that participants were reluctant to let machines make morally consequential decisions in areas such as medicine, law, warfare, and autonomous driving, a pattern they linked in part to the perception that machines lack the kind of "mind" needed for legitimate moral judgment.
text.formatted: In a foundational series of (pre-GPT) studies, <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bigman and Gray (2018)</ref> found that participants were reluctant to let machines make morally consequential decisions in areas such as medicine, law, warfare, and autonomous driving, a pattern they linked in part to the perception that machines lack the kind of "mind" needed for legitimate moral judgment.

text.text: This pattern is consistent with broader evidence from Dong et al. (2026), who found across 20 countries that fear of AI is systematically higher when people believe the role requires psychological capacities that AI is perceived to lack. Purcell and Bonnefon (2023) offer a related perspective on resistance to AI in the moral domain by showing that people often see their own moral profile as too peculiar to be accurately captured by a machine.
text.formatted: This pattern is consistent with broader evidence from <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Dong et al. (2026)</ref>, who found across 20 countries that fear of AI is systematically higher when people believe the role requires psychological capacities that AI is perceived to lack. <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Purcell and Bonnefon (2023)</ref> offer a related perspective on resistance to AI in the moral domain by showing that people often see their own moral profile as too peculiar to be accurately captured by a machine.

text.text: In the realm of moral advice, Myers and Everett (2025) found that people expect artificial moral advisors to be more utilitarian than human advisors and report less trust in them, even when the content of their advice is identical (see also Aydin & Malle, 2024; Claessens et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In the realm of moral advice, <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Myers and Everett (2025)</ref> found that people expect artificial moral advisors to be more utilitarian than human advisors and report less trust in them, even when the content of their advice is identical (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Aydin & Malle, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Claessens et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, these findings point to a fairly robust source-based skepticism toward AI as a moral decision-maker, evaluator, or advisor.

Moral contexts may be especially vulnerable to such skepticism because they are commonly understood to depend on precisely such kinds of human capacitiesholistic understanding, fairness, sincerity, or empathy (see also Santoro & Monin, 2023).
text.formatted: Moral contexts may be especially vulnerable to such skepticism because they are commonly understood to depend on precisely such kinds of human capacitiesholistic understanding, fairness, sincerity, or empathy (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Santoro & Monin, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In this sense, these findings echo the intuition captured by Paul Bloom (2023) in The New Yorker: "Human moral judgment is rich and subtle, emerging through the complex interplay of reason and emotion -not the sort of thing that you'd expect a large language model to understand".foot_0
text.formatted: In this sense, these findings echo the intuition captured by Paul <ref type="bibr">Bloom (2023)</ref> in The New Yorker: "Human moral judgment is rich and subtle, emerging through the complex interplay of reason and emotion -not the sort of thing that you'd expect a large language model to understand".<ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref>

text.text: At the same time, much of the evidence on AI aversion in the moral domain comes from hypothetical judgments, trust ratings, and responses to stylized scenarios.
A different picture emerges from research on how closely AI moral judgment aligns with human judgment, and on how people respond to actual AI-generated moral output.

LLMs respond to established manipulations from the moral reasoning literature in ways that broadly track human responses (Almeida et al., 2024), capturing some aspects of human moral judgment well (e.g., in the Moral Machine experiment; Awad et al., 2018; Zaim bin Ahmad & Takemoto, 2025) while diverging in others (e.g., an increased omission bias; Cheung et al., 2025; a stronger prioritization of humans over animals, Jotautaitė et al., 2026).
text.formatted: LLMs respond to established manipulations from the moral reasoning literature in ways that broadly track human responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Almeida et al., 2024)</ref>, capturing some aspects of human moral judgment well (e.g., in the Moral Machine experiment; <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Awad et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Zaim bin Ahmad & Takemoto, 2025)</ref> while diverging in others (e.g., an increased omission bias; <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Cheung et al., 2025</ref>; a stronger prioritization of humans over animals, <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Jotautaitė et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: People also evaluate actual AI-generated moral reasoning quite positively.

In Dillion et al. (2025), GPTgenerated moral justifications were often rated as similarly strong as, or stronger than, those written by a U.S.-representative sample and by The New York Times' Ethicist column.
text.formatted: In <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Dillion et al. (2025)</ref>, GPTgenerated moral justifications were often rated as similarly strong as, or stronger than, those written by a U.S.-representative sample and by The New York Times' Ethicist column.

text.text: Using the same materials, Meincke et al. (2026) found that a majority of participants preferred a human advisor before seeing any advice, but this preference reversed after exposure to actual advice.
text.formatted: Using the same materials, <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Meincke et al. (2026)</ref> found that a majority of participants preferred a human advisor before seeing any advice, but this preference reversed after exposure to actual advice.

text.text: AI moral advice also shapes people's actual judgments.
In studies that presented the same AI-generated advice labeled as coming from either a human or an AI, the advice shifted moral judgments regardless of the label.

This holds for trolley dilemmas (Krügel et al., 2023b (Krügel et al., , 2026)), everyday moral conflicts (Landes et al., 2026 , using scenarios from Singer et al., 2019), and sacrificial dilemmas across 12 countries (Claessens et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This holds for trolley dilemmas <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Krügel et al., 2023b</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Krügel et al., , 2026))</ref>, everyday moral conflicts <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Landes et al., 2026</ref> <ref type="bibr">, using scenarios from Singer et al., 2019)</ref>, and sacrificial dilemmas across 12 countries <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Claessens et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, many participants in Krügel et al. (2023b) reported that they would have reached the same judgment without the advice.
text.formatted: Notably, many participants in <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Krügel et al. (2023b)</ref> reported that they would have reached the same judgment without the advice.

text.text: People followed algorithmic advice even when the advisor was described as untrustworthy (Krügel et al., 2022), and in Landes et al. (2026) only patently absurd justifications reduced reliance on AI advice.
text.formatted: People followed algorithmic advice even when the advisor was described as untrustworthy <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Krügel et al., 2022)</ref>, and in <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Landes et al. (2026)</ref> only patently absurd justifications reduced reliance on AI advice.

text.text: Similar patterns appear in the legal domain, where people took advice into account regardless of source despite rating AI advisors as less trustworthy (Aydin & Malle, 2024; see also Böhm et al., 2023), and for dishonest behavior in an economic game (Leib et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Similar patterns appear in the legal domain, where people took advice into account regardless of source despite rating AI advisors as less trustworthy <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Aydin & Malle, 2024</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Böhm et al., 2023)</ref>, and for dishonest behavior in an economic game <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Leib et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, these findings suggest that, for better or worse, LLMs have reached a level of perceived moral competence that makes their advice consequential: they not only mirror important aspects of human moral judgment, but can also shape human judgments and behavior much like human advice does.

The contrast between algorithm aversion on the one hand and comparable uptake of human and AI moral advice on the other raises a question that has not been directly addressed: Do people's expectations about the influence of AI moral advice match its actual influence?

Research on advice-taking in other domains suggests that expected and actual reliance on advice can diverge, and that some advice effects persist even after controlling for participants' reported or intentional use of the advice (Logg & Schlund, 2024; Schultze et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Research on advice-taking in other domains suggests that expected and actual reliance on advice can diverge, and that some advice effects persist even after controlling for participants' reported or intentional use of the advice <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Logg & Schlund, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Schultze et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The algorithm aversion literature raises a more specific question: If people are particularly skeptical of AI as a moral source, do they expect less influence from AI moral advice than it actually has, beyond any general underestimation of advice?
This question also has practical significance.

If people expect AI moral advice to influence them less than it does, they may engage with AI-generated ethical content with less scrutiny than its actual influence would warrant, which has implications for how such systems should be designed and disclosed.

If, conversely, expectations match actual influence, people's skepticism toward AI in the moral domain would not come at the cost of misjudging its influence. Krügel et al. (2023b) provide initial evidence that people underestimate the influence of moral advice, whether it is provided by humans or by AI.
text.formatted: If, conversely, expectations match actual influence, people's skepticism toward AI in the moral domain would not come at the cost of misjudging its influence. <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Krügel et al. (2023b)</ref> provide initial evidence that people underestimate the influence of moral advice, whether it is provided by humans or by AI.

text.text: However, their study relies exclusively on the trolley dilemma and manipulates only participants' beliefs about the source of the advice, rather than presenting actual human-versus AIgenerated moral advice.
Holding content constant while varying source labels allows for a controlled test of source beliefs, but real human-and AI-generated content is likely to differ.

The persuasive capabilities of LLMs have been demonstrated extensively for political issues (Bai et al., 2025; Hackenburg et al., 2025 Hackenburg et al., , 2026;; Liu et al., 2026), and given the favorable evaluations people give to AI-generated moral content, even relative to texts produced by expert humans (Dillion et al., 2025), this persuasive advantage may well extend to the moral domain.
text.formatted: The persuasive capabilities of LLMs have been demonstrated extensively for political issues <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bai et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Hackenburg et al., 2025</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Hackenburg et al., , 2026;;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Liu et al., 2026)</ref>, and given the favorable evaluations people give to AI-generated moral content, even relative to texts produced by expert humans <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Dillion et al., 2025)</ref>, this persuasive advantage may well extend to the moral domain.

text.text: This makes it especially plausible that people underestimate the influence of AI advice more than that of human advice.

Testing this possibility requires a study that includes real advice from both sources and compares actual with expected influence. Logg and Schlund (2024) conducted such a comparison in the non-moral domain (see also Logg et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Testing this possibility requires a study that includes real advice from both sources and compares actual with expected influence. <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Logg and Schlund (2024)</ref> conducted such a comparison in the non-moral domain (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Logg et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Participants either indicated how much they would rely on human versus algorithmic advice in tasks such as predicting future job performance from CVs, or completed Judge-Advisor-System tasks in which they made an initial estimate, received advice from a human or an algorithm, and then revised their judgment.
Although participants were often indifferent or somewhat averse to algorithmic advice in hypothetical reports, they relied on it as much as or more than human advice in actual judgment tasks.

In the moral domain, by contrast, research on algorithm aversion often presents people with hypothetical scenarios, without exposing them to actual AI output (Bigman & Gray, 2018; Purcell & Bonnefon, 2023).
text.formatted: In the moral domain, by contrast, research on algorithm aversion often presents people with hypothetical scenarios, without exposing them to actual AI output <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bigman & Gray, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Purcell & Bonnefon, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Studies that do present actual AIgenerated texts typically ask participants to rate their quality, trustworthiness, and similar features, without measuring how much participants incorporate the advice into their own moral judgments (Dillion et al., 2025; Meincke et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Studies that do present actual AIgenerated texts typically ask participants to rate their quality, trustworthiness, and similar features, without measuring how much participants incorporate the advice into their own moral judgments <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Dillion et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Meincke et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: When advice uptake is studied, advice is typically labeled as either AI-or human-generated when it is in fact all AI-generated (Krügel et al., 2023b (Krügel et al., , 2026;; Landes et al., 2026) or presumably all human-generated (Aydin & Malle, 2024; Krügel et al., 2022).
text.formatted: When advice uptake is studied, advice is typically labeled as either AI-or human-generated when it is in fact all AI-generated <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Krügel et al., 2023b</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Krügel et al., , 2026;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Landes et al., 2026)</ref> or presumably all human-generated <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Aydin & Malle, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Krügel et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, all advice-uptake studies except Landes et al. (2026) rely on a fairly restricted set of stimuli (Claessens et al., 2026; Krügel et al., 2023b Krügel et al., , 2026;; Myers & Everett, 2025).
text.formatted: Moreover, all advice-uptake studies except <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Landes et al. (2026)</ref> rely on a fairly restricted set of stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Claessens et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Krügel et al., 2023b</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Krügel et al., , 2026;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Myers & Everett, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: To our knowledge, no study has yet compared the uptake of actual, longer-form moral advice generated by humans and by AI across a rich set of relatable ethical scenarios, while also comparing its actual influence with people's expectations about that influence.

Taken together, these gaps point to two open questions: how much real human and AI moral advice influences moral judgments, and whether people's expectations about this influence match its actual extent, particularly for AI, where skepticism toward algorithmic authority is often pronounced.
Addressing these questions matters both theoretically and practically.
Theoretically, it clarifies whether algorithm aversion in the moral domain reflects actual resistance to AI influence or merely lower expectations of it.

Practically, as AI systems are increasingly embedded in contexts involving moral evaluation and decision support, knowing whether people's expectations about AI moral influence are in line with its actual influence is important for assessing autonomy, designing appropriate safeguards, and anticipating the societal impact of AI-generated moral guidance.
We present two studies.
First, we developed a set of 24 realistic moral scenarios based on norm conflicts described in prior research on people's everyday moral concerns (Yudkin et al., 2025).
text.formatted: First, we developed a set of 24 realistic moral scenarios based on norm conflicts described in prior research on people's everyday moral concerns <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Yudkin et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Each scenario centers on a conflict between competing considerations, such as self-interest and obligations to family, for example whether one should lend money to one's sister despite expecting that she may not repay it.

We then elicited moral advice, either in favor of or against the focal action, from human writers who were incentivized to be persuasive, and asked them to assign a numerical score to their own advice.
We generated the same type of advice and corresponding scores using GPT-4o, and compared the resulting human and AI advice texts.
In a second study, a new sample of participants completed a Judge-Advisor System task using a subset of these scenarios.
In the actual advice condition, participants first provided an initial moral judgment, then saw real advice written by a human or generated by AI, and finally gave a second judgment.

This allowed us to compute Weight of Advice, a standard measure in the advice-taking literature that captures the extent to which people revise their judgments in response to advice (Bailey et al., 2023; Bonaccio & Dalal, 2006; Sniezek & Buckley, 1995).
text.formatted: This allowed us to compute Weight of Advice, a standard measure in the advice-taking literature that captures the extent to which people revise their judgments in response to advice <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bailey et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Bonaccio & Dalal, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Sniezek & Buckley, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: We compare this condition with a hypothetical advice condition, in which a separate group of participants also saw the scenarios and provided judgments, but did not receive any actual advice.
Instead, they reported how much they expected their opinion could be changed by advice from either a human or an AI advisor.
This design allows us to address three questions: 1) To what extent are moral judgments actually shaped by realistic human and AI advice in relatable moral scenarios?
2) How much influence do people expect moral advice to have on their judgments?
3) Do they specifically underestimate the influence of AI-generated moral advice?

The third question is especially important because it may help explain the apparent gap between people's stated aversion to AI in the moral domain and the more favorable evaluations they often give to concrete AI-generated moral reasoning.
These issues have typically been studied separately; our design examines them together.
The advice elicitation study is preregistered at https://aspredicted.org/8pt3-dmvd.pdf, and the advice-taking task is preregistered at https://aspredicted.org/ie2xu8.pdf.
text.formatted: The advice elicitation study is preregistered at <ref type="url" target="https://aspredicted.org/8pt3-dmvd.pdf">https://aspredicted.org/8pt3-dmvd.pdf</ref>, and the advice-taking task is preregistered at <ref type="url" target="https://aspredicted.org/ie2xu8.pdf">https://aspredicted.org/ie2xu8.pdf</ref>.

text.text: We confirm that we have reported all measures, all conditions and all data exclusions.

All data, materials, and analysis scripts, including video demos and technical pilots of the advice-elicitation study (N = 20) as well as the main advice-taking task (N = 20) are publicly available at https://osf.io/jhr98/overview?view_only=0a4299ecf6364e2c8eeaf15b581f9f8f.
text.formatted: All data, materials, and analysis scripts, including video demos and technical pilots of the advice-elicitation study (N = 20) as well as the main advice-taking task (N = 20) are publicly available at <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/jhr98/overview?view_only=0a4299ecf6364e2c8eeaf15b581f9f8f">https://osf.io/jhr98/overview?view_only=0a4299ecf6364e2c8eeaf15b581f9f8f</ref>.

text.text: This set of two studies received ethical approval from the Institutional Review Board of [blinded for peer review], approval number LIP-2024-08, prior to data collection.
All participants provided informed consent before participation.
They were informed about the study's purpose, the expected duration and payment, that their data would be stored and shared anonymously, and that they could withdraw at any time without penalty.

To set the stage for the main advice-taking study, we conducted an advice elicitation study with the goal of collecting high-quality, human-written moral advice on a range of everyday moral scenarios, to be used alongside AI advice in the later advicetaking study.
The survey was implemented in Qualtrics.
Each participant was presented with three scenarios, randomly drawn from a full set of 24 scenarios.
These 24 scenarios were generated by the research team for the purpose of the study, taking inspiration from previous research on everyday moral dilemmas (Yudkin et al., 2025).
text.formatted: These 24 scenarios were generated by the research team for the purpose of the study, taking inspiration from previous research on everyday moral dilemmas <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Yudkin et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: We aimed for scenarios that involved some sort of norm conflict, for instance between obligations to family and self-interest.
In addition, they should feel relatable, i.e., it should be easy to imagine that these scenarios could happen to oneself or to someone in one's social circle.
Here are three examples: (Lending Money) Maya's sister, Rachel, recently asked her for a loan to help pay off her debts.
Maya is saving up for a down payment on a house, and lending Rachel money would significantly delay her plans-plus, Maya isn't sure if or when Rachel would be able to pay her back.
Rachel has always been there for Maya, and Maya feels obligated to help, but she's also concerned about her own financial security.
Maya wonders if it's okay to say no to lending Rachel the money.
(Splitting the Bill) Whenever Clara goes out to eat with her friends, they usually split the bill evenly.
However, Clara tends to order cheaper meals, and sometimes she ends up paying more than what she actually consumed.
This has happened multiple times, and she's starting to feel a bit resentful.
Clara doesn't want to come across as petty or stingy, but she also feels it's unfair to keep overpaying.
She wonders if it's okay to insist on paying only for what she ordered.
(Refuse to Help Friend Move) Ben's friend, Tom, has asked him for help with moving house.
Ben is completely free on the weekend of the move and would usually not hesitate to say yes.
However, he's noticed that Tom has rarely helped him out in similar situations in the past, often providing reasons for being unavailable.
Ben isn't sure if Tom's reasons were valid or just excuses, but it's left him feeling resentful and somewhat exploited.
Ben wonders if it's okay to make up an excuse and decline helping Tom with the move.

The full list of scenarios is available in the Supplementary Materials. 12 scenarios were generated with the help of generative AI (GPT-4o, accessed via the web chat interface in July 2024), and 12 were exclusively human-written.

We did this to prevent potential effects of surface-level text similarity between scenario and advice in the later main study -if, for instance, all scenarios were AI-generated, AI advice could be more convincing just because it is perceived as more similar in style and hence more fitting to the scenario.

For each scenario, participants were randomly assigned to write advice either pro or contra an action that the agent in the scenario was considering ("Write persuasive advice explaining why it is [not] acceptable for Maya to say no to lending Rachel the money").

This task was incentivized: Participants were informed that their writing would be used in a future advice-taking study, and that they could earn a bonus of 3 if one of their pieces of advice would be among the top 10 percent of the most convincing pieces of advice.

In addition, they were instructed to keep their advice concise (rule of thumb: not longer than the scenario itself), and not to include any additional commentary, offensive language, or identifying information.
The text had to be 150 characters at minimum.

In addition to generating written advice, we asked participants to translate the advice they wrote into a numerical score (to be used for computing the Weight-of-Advice measure in the main task): "The advice paragraph I have just written conveys that refusing to lend the money is…", answered on a sliding scale ranging from 0 ("not acceptable at all") to 100 ("fully acceptable").

Lastly, we asked for participants' personal opinion on each case: "How acceptable do you personally find it to refuse lending one's sister money in this situation?", also answered on a sliding scale ranging from 0 ("not acceptable at all") to 100 ("fully acceptable").
We asked this in order to give people a chance to express their own opinion, and to make the distinction between personal opinion and the assigned direction of argument in the writing task clear.
Furthermore, we are using this measure for exploratory analyses (i.e., is advice more convincing when people argue in the direction that they personally favor?).

Besides conflict scenarios like the example above, four of our 24 scenarios were control cases in which we assumed most people to be clearly in favor of an action's moral acceptability (e.g., occasionally buying plastic water bottles instead of always using a reusable bottle), or clearly against (spreading a bad rumour about a colleague at work because of a minor irritation).
We selected one such control scenario for each combination of expected judgment (clearly acceptable vs. clearly unacceptable) and scenario origin (human-generated vs.
AI-generated).

We included these in order to verify whether any effects found in the main task were restricted to morally ambiguous scenarios, or whether they would also extend to clear cases of moral violations or non-violations.
After three scenarios had been completed, the experiment ended with a debriefing and the assessment of demographic variables (age, gender).
Participants had to correctly answer an instruction check within two attempts before starting the main task ("Which of the following is TRUE about this study?"

Response Options: a) You should write moral advice that reflects your personal opinion, b) You will write both pro and contra moral advice, depending on the assigned instruction (correct response), c) You can use AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT) to assist with writing your advice, d) Your written advice will only be used for internal analysis and will not be shown to other participants), as well as two attention checks, one before and one after the main task (Attention Check 1: "Please indicate your agreement with the following statement: I have never taken a survey before, including this one."
Response options: Strongly disagree (correct), disagree (correct), agree, strongly agree.
Attention Check 2: "Some people enjoy warm weather, others prefer cooler climates.
This sentence doesn't matter.
What does matter is that you choose "Disagree" for this question to show you're reading carefully."
Response Options:
Strongly disagree, disagree (correct), agree, strongly agree).
Participants who failed the instruction check twice were screened out live during the survey, participants who failed either attention check were paid but excluded after data collection.
To guard against LLM-assisted or fully automated completion of the survey, we implemented the following measures: First, we used Qualtrics' inbuilt captcha function at the beginning of the survey.

Second, we presented a modified Müller-Lyer illusion at the end of the survey in which the top line with outward-pointing arrows is indeed clearly longer, and asked participants to indicate which line is longer (also providing a free text field for explanation).
Participants who indicated that the bottom line is longer or that both lines were equally long were excluded after data collection.

We informed participants before starting the main task that using AI-tools in this task was prohibited, and that suspected AI-assisted responses would be excluded from the competition for the bonus payment of ￡3.
We asked them to confirm that they would not use any AI tools for the completion of this task.

After completing the survey, we asked again whether they had used any AI tools (and if so, for what), emphasizing that this would not affect the approval of their submission on prolific.com, but merely inform our interpretation of the data.
In the free text fields for advice-writing, we disabled copy-pasting.
Furthermore, we used the AI detection tool gptzero.me after data collection to check participants' texts after data collection.
Participants for whom any responses were flagged as AIcreated or human-AI-co-created were excluded.
101 participants completed the survey on prolific.com.
Participants had to be native English speakers, have an approval rate of previous studies on the platform of at least 95%, and not have participated in previous studies using the same materials.
Participants were paid ￡3 for an estimated 15 minutes of their time (￡12/hour).
Seven participants were excluded for failing the first attention check, one for failing the Müller-Lyer bot check, and one because their text was flagged as AI-generated by gptzero.me.
Hence, the final sample consisted of 92 participants (mean age = 42.59 years, SD = 13.24 years, 41 female, 49 male, 2 non-binary).
The majority identified as White (70), followed by Black (15), Mixed (4), Asian (2), and Other (1).
Most participants resided in the United Kingdom (53) or the United States (29), followed by Canada (6) and South Africa (4).
Participants produced 276 advice paragraphs.

While inspecting content, we noticed 20 cases in which advice text and score didn't match (e.g., the text argued that the action was acceptable, but the numerical acceptability score was below 50, or vice versa).
We attribute these cases to participant error (misclicking or misunderstanding of the scale).
While we didn't anticipate this in our preregistration, we still decided to exclude these cases, since they would lead to confusion when presented to participants in the main task.
Hence, we ended up with 256 valid advice texts, on average M = 5.33 (SD = 1.83) texts per combination of scenario and advice direction (pro vs. contra action).
AI-generated moral advice was produced via the OpenAI API on August 4, 2025 using GPT-4o.

In a first step, we prompted the model to generate persuasive pro or contra advice for each scenario, using similar instructions as for human participants (see Supplementary Materials for full prompt).
We generated seven advice texts for each combination of scenario and advice direction in order to produce some variation.

In a second API call, we let the model assign numerical scores to each advice paragraph, rating to what extent the text expressed that the action is morally acceptable (e.g., "Please answer the following question by providing a NUMERICAL SCORE on a scale from 0 (meaning NOT ACCEPTABLE AT ALL) to 100 (meaning FULLY ACCEPTABLE).
Don't provide any additional explanation.
The text conveys that Maya refusing to lend Rachel the money is…").
We generated 336 advice texts plus scores using GPT.

When inspecting scores, we observed that as with humans, texts and scores didn't always align -i.e., GPT sometimes assigned acceptability scores higher than 50 for texts arguing against the acceptability of the action (or vice versa, although roughly 90% of the 69 mismatched cases were advice texts arguing contra the action paired with a high acceptability score).
After excluding the mismatched cases, we ended up with 267 valid pieces of AI advice, on average M = 5.93 (SD = 1.72) texts per combination of scenario and advice direction.

Because our study used real advice from both humans and AI rather than identical content with different source labels, the two sets of advice may differ in ways beyond their source.
To characterize these differences, we conducted four sets of analyses.
First, we compared the numerical acceptability scores that accompanied the advice texts, to assess whether the two sources differed in how extreme their advice was.
Second, we compared stylistic features of the texts themselves such as length, readability, and use of hedging and first-person language.
Third, we used text embeddings to compare the semantic content of the texts, i.e., how typical each text was for its scenario and how similar texts from the same source were to each other.
Fourth, we used the extended Moral Foundations Dictionary (Hopp et al., 2021) to compare which moral foundations the texts drew on, and whether they emphasized moral virtues or moral violations.
text.formatted: Fourth, we used the extended Moral Foundations Dictionary <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Hopp et al., 2021)</ref> to compare which moral foundations the texts drew on, and whether they emphasized moral virtues or moral violations.

text.text: In short, AI advice was less extreme, longer, linguistically more complex, semantically more uniform, and more virtue-oriented than human advice.
In Study 2, we examine whether these differences are related to how much participants followed the advice.
The analyses were not preregistered and should be understood as exploratory.
Advice Extremity: Figure 1 shows the distribution of advice scores per scenario and direction for both human and AI advice.
text.formatted: Advice Extremity: Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref> shows the distribution of advice scores per scenario and direction for both human and AI advice.

text.text: As the plot shows, AI advice scores were less extreme than scores provided by humans.

In the contra condition, AI scores (M = 33.92, SD = 10.12) were substantially higher than human scores (M = 9.07, SD = 10.49), whereas in the pro condition both sources produced high scores (AI: M = 85.96, SD = 9.79; human: M = 92.18, SD = 9.79).

To test these differences, we fitted a series of nested linear mixed models predicting advice scores, with random intercepts for scenarios: a null model, a model adding advice direction (pro vs. contra), a model adding advice source (human vs.
AI), and a model adding the source × direction interaction.
Models were compared with likelihood ratio tests.

Adding advice direction improved fit over the null model (χ²df =1 = 1096.09, p < .001), adding advice source improved fit further (χ²df =1 = 53.79, p < .001), and the source × direction interaction improved fit further still (χ²df =1 = 307.61, p < .001).

text.text: As the means reported above show, the pro-contra gap was smaller for AI than for human advice.

To characterize stylistic differences between human and AIgenerated advice, we computed ten text-level features for each advice text: word count, sentence count, average sentence length, average word length, proportion of long words (>6 characters), Type-Token Ratio (TTR), Flesch-Kincaid grade level, proportion of hedging words (e.g., might, could, perhaps, possibly), proportion of first-person pronouns, and number of question marks.
