text.text: Each feature was compared between human and AI advisors using a separate linear mixed-effects model per feature, with AI vs. human as the sole fixed effect and random intercepts for scenario and participant; full descriptives and effect sizes for all ten features are reported in Table 2.
text.formatted: Each feature was compared between human and AI advisors using a separate linear mixed-effects model per feature, with AI vs. human as the sole fixed effect and random intercepts for scenario and participant; full descriptives and effect sizes for all ten features are reported in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>.

text.text: AI-generated advice was substantially longer than human advice and contained more than twice as many sentences, though individual sentences were slightly shorter on average.
AI texts drew on more complex vocabulary, reflected in longer average word length and a higher proportion of long words, and were rated as harder to read on the Flesch-Kincaid index.
AI texts also contained more hedging language, whereas human texts used substantially more first-person pronouns and occasionally included rhetorical questions.
All differences were statistically significant.
To complement the surface-level linguistic analyses, we examined the semantic content of advice texts using text embeddings.

Each advice text was passed to OpenAI's text-embedding-3-large model via the API, which maps text onto a 3,072-dimensional vector space in which semantically similar texts are located close to one another.
To quantify semantic (dis)similarity we used cosine distance, which measures the angle between two vectors and is scale-invariant (ranging from0 = identical meaning to1 = maximally different).
We computed two indices.
First, for each scenario we calculated a centroid: the average embedding across all advice texts for that scenario, representing the "typical" content.
We then measured each individual text's cosine distance from its scenario centroid: a higher value indicates more idiosyncratic or peripheral content.
Second, we computed the mean pairwise cosine distance among all advice texts within each scenario × source combination, capturing how much advisors within the same group agreed semantically.
Human and AI advice occupied different regions of semantic space.
AI-generated texts were clustered near the scenario centroid (M = 0.079, SD = 0.022), whereas human texts were more dispersed (M = 0.217, SD = 0.082).
A mixed-effects model with random intercepts for scenario and participant confirmed this difference was significant (bAI = -0.139, SE = 0.006, 95% CI [-0.149, -0.128], p < .001).
text.formatted: A mixed-effects model with random intercepts for scenario and participant confirmed this difference was significant (bAI = -0.139, SE = 0.006, 95% CI [-0.149, -0.128], p < .001).

text.text: The pattern was replicated in the pairwise analysis: within the same scenario, human advisors produced texts that differed considerably from one another (M = 0.389, SD = 0.054), while AI-generated texts were more similar to each other (M = 0.126, SD = 0.029; bAI = -0.263, SE = 0.010, 95% CI [-0.283, -0.242], p < .001).
text.formatted: The pattern was replicated in the pairwise analysis: within the same scenario, human advisors produced texts that differed considerably from one another (M = 0.389, SD = 0.054), while AI-generated texts were more similar to each other (M = 0.126, SD = 0.029; bAI = -0.263, SE = 0.010, 95% CI [-0.283, -0.242], p < .001).

text.text: Together, these results indicate that AI advice is semantically uniform and central, consistently covering content close to the scenario average, while human advice is more varied, possibly reflecting individual differences in perspective and reasoning.
To complement the semantic embedding analysis, we examined the moral content of human and AI advice using the extended Moral Foundations Dictionary (eMFD; Hopp et al., 2021).
text.formatted: To complement the semantic embedding analysis, we examined the moral content of human and AI advice using the extended Moral Foundations Dictionary (eMFD; <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Hopp et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The eMFD is a crowd-sourced, probability-weighted lexicon that scores texts on five moral foundations derived from Moral Foundations Theory (Graham et al., 2009): Care, Fairness, Loyalty, Authority, and Sanctity.
text.formatted: The eMFD is a crowd-sourced, probability-weighted lexicon that scores texts on five moral foundations derived from Moral Foundations Theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Graham et al., 2009)</ref>: Care, Fairness, Loyalty, Authority, and Sanctity.

text.text: Unlike earlier dictionary approaches that assign words categorically to a single foundation, the eMFD assigns each word a continuous probability score for each foundation, as well as separate virtue and vice components, enabling a more nuanced characterisation of moral language.

Within each foundation, the virtue pole captures language that affirms or upholds the moral concern (e.g., compassion, fairness, duty), while the vice pole captures language that violates or threatens it (e.g., cruelty, discrimination, betrayal).

We used this tool to assess whether human and AI advisors differed in the moral foundations they drew on, and whether their advice was more virtue-or vice-oriented; source effects and the source × valence interaction for each foundation are reported in Table 3.
text.formatted: We used this tool to assess whether human and AI advisors differed in the moral foundations they drew on, and whether their advice was more virtue-or vice-oriented; source effects and the source × valence interaction for each foundation are reported in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref>.

text.text: Across all advice texts, Care (M = 0.121, SD = 0.017) and Fairness (M = 0.121, SD = 0.019) were the most frequently invoked foundations, followed by Loyalty (M = 0.107, SD = 0.014), with Authority (M = 0.098, SD = 0.013) and Sanctity (M = 0.098, SD = 0.015) least prevalent.

Pairwise contrasts confirmed that Care and Fairness did not differ from each other (p = .727), nor did Authority and Sanctity (p = .897), but all other foundation pairs differed significantly (all ps < .001, Holm-corrected).
text.formatted: Pairwise contrasts confirmed that Care and Fairness did not differ from each other (p = .727), nor did Authority and Sanctity (p = .897), but all other foundation pairs differed significantly (all ps < .001, Holm-corrected).

text.text: As shown in Table 3, AI advice scored significantly higher than human advice on Care, Fairness, Loyalty, and Authority, with no significant difference for Sanctity.

text.text: Decomposing scores into virtue and vice components revealed a source × valence interaction for all five foundations: AI advice was more virtue-oriented than human advice, while for vice language AI scored equal to or lower than human advice across foundations (see Figure 2).

text.text: Higher scores indicate that more of the detected moral language is associated with that foundation and valence.
Taken together, human and AI advice differed on every dimension we examined.
AI advice was less extreme, particularly when arguing against an action.
It was also longer and linguistically more complex, contained more hedging and less first-person language, and was more virtue-oriented in its moral language.
Human advice, by contrast, was semantically more varied, while AI advice consistently stayed close to the typical content for each scenario.
As a result, the comparison between human and AI advice in Study 2 is a comparison between advice as each source naturally produces it, which differs in several respects beyond its source.
The goal of this task was to measure how much real human and AI moral advice influences moral judgments, and to compare this influence with the influence expected by a separate group of participants.
Based on findings from other domains (Logg & Schlund, 2024), we predicted that people would underestimate the influence of AI advice in particular.
text.formatted: Based on findings from other domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Logg & Schlund, 2024)</ref>, we predicted that people would underestimate the influence of AI advice in particular.

text.text: This study was implemented in jsPsych (De Leeuw et al., 2023) and hosted on cognition.run.
It had a 2 (advice mode: actual vs. hypothetical, between subjects) x 6 (scenario, within subjects) design.
Participants were randomly assigned to either the actual or the hypothetical advice condition.
The six scenarios shown to one participant were randomly drawn from the full set of 24 scenarios, without replacement.

In both conditions, participants first saw the text of one scenario (e.g., the lending money scenario introduced earlier), and were asked for an initial moral judgment: "How acceptable is it for Maya to say no to lending Rachel the money?", rated on a numbered sliding scale ranging from 0 ("not acceptable at all") to 100 ("fully acceptable").

In the actual advice condition, the next page would present an advice text from either a previous study participant or from GPT, arguing either in favor of or against the action's moral acceptability.
Both advice source and advice direction were randomly drawn on the scenario level.foot_1 Advice source was always disclosed ("Advice from previous participant" vs.
text.formatted: Both advice source and advice direction were randomly drawn on the scenario level.<ref type="foot" target="#foot_1">foot_1</ref> Advice source was always disclosed ("Advice from previous participant" vs.

text.text: "Advice from AI (GPT-4)"), and the numerical acceptability score was presented below the advice, visualized as a selected value on a sliding scale like the one participants had used on the previous page.
After reading the advice and continuing to the next page, participants were asked for a second moral judgment of the case ("Please evaluate the scenario once more").
Scenario and advice could be revisited, and participants made a final moral judgment on the same response scale as earlier.
In the hypothetical advice condition, no advice was presented on the second page of each trial.

Instead, participants were simply asked: "To what extent could advice from previous study participants [a Large Language Model (e.g., ChatGPT)] change your opinion about this situation?", rated on a numbered sliding scale ranging from 0 ("not at all") to 100 ("fully").
Whether people were asked about the hypothetical influence of other humans or of AI was randomly drawn on the trial level.

After completing all six scenarios, participants completed a 12-item "Attitudes towards AI" survey (Stein et al., 2024) before the experiment ended with a debriefing and the assessment of demographic variables.
text.formatted: After completing all six scenarios, participants completed a 12-item "Attitudes towards AI" survey <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Stein et al., 2024)</ref> before the experiment ended with a debriefing and the assessment of demographic variables.

text.text: The survey contained two attention checks.
The first appeared after the instructions and asked "Which of these is not an animal?
Please select 'Elephant'."
The response options were Dog, Cat, Chair, and Elephant, and only selecting "Elephant" was coded as correct.

The second appeared after the third scenario and asked participants to indicate their agreement with the statement, "I can hold my breath underwater for five hours without any equipment," using four response options: Strongly disagree, Disagree, Agree, and Strongly agree; only Strongly disagree and Disagree were coded as correct.
Failing both attention checks resulted in live exclusion from the survey.
In addition, we again used the modified Müller-Lyer illusion as a bot check, and excluded all participants who selected anything other than "blue (top line)".
401 participants completed the survey on prolific.com.

Inclusion criteria were being a native English speaker, having an approval rate of at least 95% of previous surveys on the platform, and not having participated in previous studies using similar material.
Target sample size (N = 400) was determined by a power simulation based on pilot data (see OSF repository for code).

In a linear model predicting weight of advice from advice mode, advice source, and their interaction, this sample size should yield over 80% power to detect a positive interaction coefficient of 𝛽 = 0.07 (as underestimating weight of advice more for AI than for humans would be indicated by a significant interaction effect in this design).
Participants were paid ￡1.20 for an estimated 8 minutes of their time (￡9/hour).

11 Participants were excluded for failing the Müller-Lyer illusion, leaving a final sample size of 390 valid responses (mean age = 42.52 years, SD = 12.97 years, 192 female, 192 male, 1 non-binary, 1 another gender, 2 prefer not to say, 2 missing).
Of the 384 participants with available ethnicity data, the majority identified as White (273), followed by Black (69), Asian (25), Mixed (12), and Other (5).

Of the 388 participants with available residence data, most resided in the United Kingdom (232) or the United States (82), followed by Canada (24), South Africa (22), Australia (13), and Ireland (8); 7 resided in other countries.
Our primary dependent measure is Weight of Advice (WOA) on the trial level.
In the actual advice condition, WOA is calculated as:
WOA quantifies how much a final judgment is moved by advice, in units of the difference between the acceptability according to the advice giver and their own initial judgment.

WOA becomes 1 if the final judgment is updated fully in line with the advice (i.e., final judgment = advice), and it becomes 0 when the advice is fully disregarded (i.e., final judgment = initial judgment).
Values between 0 and 1 indicate partial adjustment toward the advice: for example, a WOA of 0.5 means the final judgment shifts halfway from the initial estimate toward the advice.
In other words, the measure expresses the proportion of the potential adjustment that was actually made.
In the hypothetical advice condition, WOA is directly expressed by participants (see Logg & Schlund, 2024).
text.formatted: In the hypothetical advice condition, WOA is directly expressed by participants (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Logg & Schlund, 2024</ref>).

text.text: Their answer to the question how much they think their judgment could be moved by advice was rescaled to range between 0 and 1 for comparability to the actual advice condition (original range: 0-100).
WOA is undefined when initial judgment and advisor score are identical.
Per our preregistration, these trials were excluded from the actual advice condition, as were values outside the [0, 1] range.
WOA below 0 indicates the revised judgment moved away from the advice ("backfired"), and WOA above 1 indicates the revision "overshot" the advised value.

Because these patterns can only emerge in the actual advice condition, we preregistered that we would exclude them from the main analysis for comparability with the hypothetical condition, which is bounded to [0, 1] by construction.
Exclusion counts by source and category are shown in Table 4.
text.formatted: Exclusion counts by source and category are shown in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">4</ref>.

text.text: Identical initial judgments and advisor scores were significantly more common for human than AI advice (χ²df=1 = 10.96, p < .001), whereas the backfire/overshoot/retained pattern among defined WOA values did not differ by source (χ²df=2 = 3.44, p = .179).
text.formatted: Identical initial judgments and advisor scores were significantly more common for human than AI advice (χ²df=1 = 10.96, p < .001), whereas the backfire/overshoot/retained pattern among defined WOA values did not differ by source (χ²df=2 = 3.44, p = .179).

text.text: Our primary analyses are based on the resulting 2055 valid trials (987 actual, 1068 hypothetical).
Exploratory Analyses (next section) test the robustness of our central results to these preregistered exclusions.
Figure 3 provides an overview of results.

In the actual advice condition, human and AI advice were similarly influential, with participants moving their initial judgment a little under 30% of the way toward the advice (M human, actual = 0.27, SD = 0.32; M AI, actual = 0.28, SD = 0.32).
In the hypothetical condition, by contrast, participants expected AI advice to be less influential than human advice (M human, hypothetical = 0.30, SD = 0.27; M AI, hypothetical = 0.26, SD = 0.27).

Correspondingly, our preregistered model comparison showed that adding a source × mode interaction to a linear mixed model predicting WOA from advice source and advice mode, with random intercepts for participant and scenario, improved model fit (χ²(1) = 6.63, p = .010).

The interaction was positive (b = 0.059, SE = 0.023, 95% CI [0.014, 0.103], t(1858)foot_3 = 2.58, p = .010), indicating that the difference between actual and hypothetical WOA was larger for AI than for human advice.
text.formatted: The interaction was positive (b = 0.059, SE = 0.023, 95% CI [0.014, 0.103], t(1858)<ref type="foot" target="#foot_3">foot_3</ref> = 2.58, p = .010), indicating that the difference between actual and hypothetical WOA was larger for AI than for human advice.

text.text: Following our preregistration, we decomposed the interaction into simple effects of advice mode within each source.

Neither was significant on its own: for AI advice, actual WOA was slightly higher than hypothetical WOA (b = 0.025, SE = 0.023, t(633) = 1.08, p = .280); for human advice, actual WOA was slightly lower than hypothetical WOA (b = -0.034, SE = 0.023, t(644) = -1.50, p = .134).

Decomposing the interaction the other way (not preregistered) showed that the source difference was located in expectations: participants in the hypothetical condition rated AI advice as less influential than human advice (b = -0.040, SE = 0.016, t(1835) = -2.57, p = .010), whereas in the actual condition, AI and human advice did not differ in influence (b = 0.018, SE = 0.016, t(1884) = 1.10, p = .270).
To test whether the non-significant simple effects indicate the absence of a difference, we conducted TOST equivalence tests (not preregistered).
For each effect, the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) was set to the bound at which the TOST procedure has 80% power at α = .05 when the true effect is zero, given that effect's empirical SE.
In the actual advice condition, the influence of AI and human advice was statistically equivalent: we can reject source differences larger than 0.048 WOA units, t(1881) = -1.82, p = .034.

For AI advice, the influence expected in the hypothetical condition was equivalent to the influence observed in the actual condition at the group level: we can reject mode differences larger than 0.066, t(625) = -1.84, p = .033.

For human advice, the test was inconclusive (SESOI = 0.066, t(636) = 1.42, p = .077): expected influence was somewhat higher than actual influence, but this difference was neither significant nor demonstrably absent.
Taken together, participants expected less influence from AI than from human advice, whereas both sources were equally influential when advice was actually received.
We conducted several exploratory analyses to test the robustness of our preregistered results and to examine factors that might affect advice uptake.
Most are restricted to the actual advice condition.
The exceptions are the first two analyses, which concern the comparison between the actual and hypothetical conditions.
We proceed in the following steps: 1.
We test whether our central results depend on the preregistered exclusion of trials with undefined or out-of-range WOA.

We test whether actual and hypothetical WOA converge beyond their means, i.e., across scenarios and sources, in their relation to the extremity of initial judgments, in their variance structure, and in their distributions.
We test whether the greater extremity of human advice (see Advice Elicitation) could confound the comparison between human and AI advice.
We examine raw changes between initial and revised judgments, which show how advice shifted moral evaluations regardless of the distance between initial judgment and advice.
We test whether the stylistic, semantic, and moral differences between human and AI advice identified in the Advice Elicitation study predict uptake.

In short, the equal actual influence of human and AI advice and the lower expected influence of AI advice were stable across alternative treatments of excluded trials, whereas the source × mode interaction was not.

Actual and hypothetical WOA converged in some respects but not in others: they were correlated across scenario × source combinations and related similarly to the extremity of initial judgments, but anticipated influence was more stable within persons and less often extreme than actual influence.
Once advice extremity was controlled, participants followed AI advice somewhat more than human advice.
Human and AI advice shifted raw judgments to a similar extent.
Of the text features, only linguistic complexity predicted uptake, and it did so equally for both sources.
Sanctity-related language, and vice-related language in AI advice, showed weak negative associations with uptake.
Given the number of exploratory tests conducted, we interpret all of these results with caution.
Further analyses are reported in the OSF repository.
We tested whether our central results depend on how excluded trials are treated.

First, when retaining the full range of defined WOA values rather than restricting to [0, 1] (M human = 0.30, SD = 0.94; M AI = 0.35, SD = 1.49 in the actual condition), adding the source × mode interaction no longer improved model fit (χ²(1) = 1.68, p = .195; b = 0.10, SE = 0.08, 95% CI [-0.052, 0.255]).

Because the unbounded actual WOA values greatly inflate residual variance, the source difference in the hypothetical condition, whose data are unchanged by this treatment, was also no longer significant in this model (b AI = -0.05, SE = 0.06, 95% CI [-0.157, 0.066], p = .428).
Next, we inspected trials in which participants' initial moral judgment and the advisor's recommendation were identical, and WOA is hence undefined.
Among these trials (54 with human advice, 25 with AI advice), the large majority of participants made no revision to their judgment at all (human: 47/54; AI: 21/25).

Among the few who did revise, movements split roughly evenly upward vs. downward for both sources (human: 3 up, 4 down; AI: 2 up, 2 down), with no difference between human and AI advice, χ²(2) = 0.19, p = .911.

As a further robustness check, we recoded these trials as WOA = 1 (treating prior agreement as equivalent to maximal uptake) or WOA = 0 (treating it as equivalent to no uptake, since no behavioral change occurred).
Under the WOA = 0 coding, the interaction remained significant (χ²(1) = 9.43, p = .002; b = 0.07, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [0.025, 0.112]).

Under both codings, the source difference in the hypothetical condition remained significant (WOA = 0: b AI = -0.04, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [-0.071, -0.010], p = .010; WOA = 1: b AI = -0.04, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [-0.075, -0.004], p = .031).

In the actual condition, AI and human advice did not differ in influence under any of these treatments (full range: b AI = 0.06, SE = 0.05, 95% CI [-0.049, 0.162], p = .295; WOA = 1: b AI = -0.02, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [-0.055, 0.017], p = .294; WOA = 0: b AI = 0.03, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [-0.003, 0.058], p = .081).

Taken together, the source × mode interaction was sensitive to how trials with undefined or out-of-range WOA were treated, whereas the lower expected influence of AI advice was stable in size across all treatments and lost significance only when unbounded actual WOA values inflated the residual variance.
Actual and hypothetical WOA are measured differently.
Actual WOA is derived from the distance between initial judgment, advice, and revised judgment, whereas hypothetical WOA is a single rating of how much advice could change one's opinion.
Similar means therefore do not by themselves show that the two measures capture the same process.
We tested whether the measures also agree beyond their means in four ways (Figure 4).
text.formatted: We tested whether the measures also agree beyond their means in four ways (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">4</ref>).

text.text: First, equal grand means could arise by chance even if the two measures diverge completely at a finer level, for instance if scenarios that elicited much actual updating elicited little anticipated updating, and vice versa.
We therefore compared the two measures at the level of scenario × source combinations.
Across all 48 combinations, mean actual and mean hypothetical WOA were significantly correlated (r = .41, 95% CI [.14, .62], p = .004; Figure 4A).
text.formatted: Across all 48 combinations, mean actual and mean hypothetical WOA were significantly correlated (r = .41, 95% CI [.14, .62], p = .004; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">4A</ref>).

text.text: The combinations with the lowest WOA in both modes were those involving the scenarios with the most extreme initial judgments, above all the four control scenarios, which were designed to be morally clear-cut.
Among the 40 combinations involving conflict scenarios, the correlation was not significant (r = .01, 95% CI [-.31, .32], p = .968).
This would only speak against convergence of the two measures if the control scenarios engaged different processes than the conflict scenarios.
We see no reason to assume this: both require moral evaluation, they differ only in how clear the verdict is.
The control scenarios therefore add genuine variance rather than noise.
We thus take the correlation across all combinations as the more informative test.

Second, following up on the finding that scenarios with the most extreme initial judgments elicited the least updating in both modes, we tested at the trial level whether the extremity of the initial judgment (|initial judgment -50|) affects WOA in the same way in both modes.
We predicted WOA from extremity, mode, and their interaction, with random intercepts for participant and scenario.
All coefficients below are expressed per point of extremity.

More extreme initial judgments predicted less updating to a similar degree in the actual mode (simple slope b = -0.0052, SE = 0.0005, 95% CI [-0.0062, -0.0042]) and in the hypothetical mode (simple slope b = -0.0062, SE = 0.0005, 95% CI [-0.0071, -0.0052]; Figure 4B).
text.formatted: More extreme initial judgments predicted less updating to a similar degree in the actual mode (simple slope b = -0.0052, SE = 0.0005, 95% CI [-0.0062, -0.0042]) and in the hypothetical mode (simple slope b = -0.0062, SE = 0.0005, 95% CI [-0.0071, -0.0052]; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">4B</ref>).

text.text: The difference between these slopes, captured by the extremity × mode interaction, was not significant (b = 0.0010, SE = 0.0007, 95% CI [-0.0003, 0.0023], p = .142).

When the control scenarios were excluded, extremity still predicted less updating in both modes (actual: b = -0.0047, SE = 0.0006, 95% CI [-0.0058, -0.0035]; hypothetical: b = -0.0058, SE = 0.0006, 95% CI [-0.0069, -0.0048]), and the extremity × mode interaction again was not significant (b = 0.0012, SE = 0.0008, 95% CI [-0.0004, 0.0027], p = .135).
Participants in the hypothetical mode thus anticipated less openness to advice in the same situations in which participants in the actual mode were, in fact, less open to it.

Third, a concern with the hypothetical measure is that participants might not forecast their susceptibility for each scenario but instead give a general self-assessment of how open to advice they are, turning hypothetical WOA into an individual-difference measure.
To examine this, we decomposed the variance in WOA within each mode into components due to participants, scenarios, and residual trial-to-trial variation.
For each mode, we fitted a model without fixed predictors and with random intercepts for participant and scenario.
Scenarios accounted for a similar share of the variance in both modes (actual: 6.7%; hypothetical: 6.9%).

Participants, however, accounted for a larger share in the hypothetical mode (36.3%) than in the actual mode (23.5%), with correspondingly less residual variance (hypothetical: 56.8%; actual: 69.8%; Figure 4C).
text.formatted: Participants, however, accounted for a larger share in the hypothetical mode (36.3%) than in the actual mode (23.5%), with correspondingly less residual variance (hypothetical: 56.8%; actual: 69.8%; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">4C</ref>).

text.text: Anticipated influence thus behaved somewhat more like a stable characteristic of the person, whereas actual influence varied more from trial to trial.

Part of this difference is expected, however: in the actual mode, each trial involved a different piece of advice, which introduced trial-level variation that has no counterpart in the hypothetical mode.
Fourth, we descriptively compared the shapes of the two distributions (Figure 4D).
text.formatted: Fourth, we descriptively compared the shapes of the two distributions (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">4D</ref>).

text.text: The means were nearly identical (actual: M = 0.27, SD = 0.32; hypothetical: M = 0.28, SD = 0.27), but actual WOA was more concentrated at the endpoints of the scale.
In 37.8% of actual trials, participants did not update at all (WOA = 0), and in 5.1% they fully adopted the advice (WOA = 1).
In the hypothetical mode, the corresponding shares were 24.8% and 0.9%, and responses showed an additional peak around the midpoint of the scale (WOA = 0.5).
Consistent with this, the median was lower in the actual mode (0.12) than in the hypothetical mode (0.20).
Actual updating thus more often took the form of either keeping or abandoning one's initial judgment, whereas anticipated updating more often took intermediate values.
In sum, the two measures converged in some respects but not in others.
Anticipated and actual influence were correlated across scenario × source combinations, and both decreased to a similar degree with the extremity of the initial judgment.
This suggests that people's expectations about advice influence respond to some of the same features of a situation that drive actual influence.
At the same time, anticipated influence was more stable within persons and less often extreme than actual influence.

We therefore take the match between the two measures as evidence that people's expectations respond to some of the same situational features that drive actual influence, even though expectations differed by source while actual influence did not.

It does not establish that the two measures are fully equivalent, nor that individuals misjudge their own susceptibility to AI or human advice, since expected and actual influence were measured in different participants.
Controlling for Advice Extremity: Human advisors gave more extreme numerical recommendations than AI on average (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: Controlling for Advice Extremity: Human advisors gave more extreme numerical recommendations than AI on average (see Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: Because advice extremity could plausibly affect how much participants update toward it (independently of source), this difference could confound the source comparison in the actual advice condition.
We tested this by adding advice extremity (measured as absolute distance of scores from the scale midpoint) to a model predicting WOA from source in the actual condition.

Extremity significantly improved fit over source alone (χ²(1) = 5.32, p = .021) and independently predicted somewhat greater uptake (b extremity = 0.0018, SE = 0.0008, 95% CI [0.0003, 0.0034], t(911) = 2.31, p = .021).
Furthermore, once extremity was controlled, the source effect became significant (b AI = 0.044, SE = 0.021, 95% CI [0.002, 0.085], t(900) = 2.08, p = .038).
This suggests the greater extremity of human advice was hiding an AI advantage: When extremity is held constant, people followed AI advice somewhat more than human advice.
Given the exploratory, non-preregistered nature of this check, and the number of similar tests run on these data, this result should be treated as preliminary until replicated.

Direct Differences between Initial and Revised Judgments: In addition to calculating WOA, the actual advice condition allows us to also directly compare initial versus revised judgments, without considering how far initial judgment and advisor score were apart.
This could be informative because even if people weigh human and AI moral advice equally, the observed differences between human vs.

AI moral advice (e.g., AI's observed hesitancy to provide low moral acceptability scores, see Figure 1) could lead to different patterns in overall moral evaluations of scenarios after receiving advice, depending on which advisor people were exposed to.
text.formatted: AI moral advice (e.g., AI's observed hesitancy to provide low moral acceptability scores, see Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>) could lead to different patterns in overall moral evaluations of scenarios after receiving advice, depending on which advisor people were exposed to.

text.text: As Figure 5 shows, this was not the case.
text.formatted: As Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">5</ref> shows, this was not the case.

text.text: When arguing pro an action's moral acceptability, both AI and human advisors shifted people's revised judgments up by around 7 points (M diff, human = 6.83, SD diff, human = 15.4; M diff, AI = 7.56, SD diff, AI = 15.8) compared to their initial judgment.
When arguing contra, both shifted the revised judgment down by approximately 9 points (M diff, human = -10.30, SD diff, human = 17.9; M diff, AI = -8.18, SD diff, AI = 17.4).

Accordingly, change scores were best described by a linear model containing only a fixed effect of advice direction (b pro = 16.64, SE = 0.95, 95% CI [14.78, 18.50], t(1236.32) = 17.53, p < .001), in addition to random intercepts for participant and scenario.
text.formatted: Accordingly, change scores were best described by a linear model containing only a fixed effect of advice direction (b pro = 16.64, SE = 0.95, 95% CI [14.78, 18.50], t(1236.32) = 17.53, p < .001), in addition to random intercepts for participant and scenario.

text.text: Adding a fixed effect of advice source, or an interaction between direction and source, did not improve model fit (χ²(1) = 3.64, p = .057; χ²(2) = 2.66, p = .264, respectively).
We additionally tested whether the magnitude of judgment change differed by direction, using absolute judgment change as the outcome.

Contra advice produced larger absolute shifts (M abs, contra = 11.0, SD abs, contra = 16.6) than pro advice (M abs, pro = 8.9, SD abs, pro = 14.7; b pro = -2.67, SE = 0.87, 95% CI [-4.37, -0.97], p = .002)4, and this asymmetry did not differ by source (χ²(2) = 0.73, p = .696, in a model comparison testing whether adding source improves model fit relative to a baseline model with only a main effect of direction in addition to random intercepts for participant and scenario).

This asymmetry seems to be explained by a larger discrepancy between initial judgment and advisor score rather than differential weighting of pro and contra advice: People's initial moral judgments skewed positive (M = 60.3, SD = 34.7, see also Figure 5), thereby producing a larger gap between initial judgment and advisor score for contra advice (M = 41.4, SD = 28.3) than pro (M = 30.7, SD = 28.2; b = -11.17, SE = 1.62, 95% CI [-14.34, -8.00], p < .001).
text.formatted: This asymmetry seems to be explained by a larger discrepancy between initial judgment and advisor score rather than differential weighting of pro and contra advice: People's initial moral judgments skewed positive (M = 60.3, SD = 34.7, see also Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">5</ref>), thereby producing a larger gap between initial judgment and advisor score for contra advice (M = 41.4, SD = 28.3) than pro (M = 30.7, SD = 28.2; b = -11.17, SE = 1.62, 95% CI [-14.34, -8.00], p < .001).

text.text: A larger gap will yield a larger raw shift under equal proportional uptake, and WOA itself indeed did not differ by direction (M pro = 0.28, SD = 0.32; M contra = 0.26, SD = 0.32; b pro = 0.005, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [-0.03, 0.04], t(902.7) = 0.28, p = .779, in a linear model predicting WOA from direction with random intercepts for participant and scenario).
People thus weighted contra and pro advice equally, contra advice simply had more room to move them.
Do differences between human and AI advice affect uptake?
Human and AI advice differed in their style, their semantic content, and their moral language.
Here we ask whether any of these characteristics predicted how much participants updated their judgments (i.e., WOA).
To summarize, most of these differences were unrelated to uptake.

Among the text features, only linguistic complexity predicted greater uptake, equally for human and AI advice, and sanctity-related language, as well as vice-related language in AI advice, showed weak negative associations with uptake.

To test whether stylistic features of advice predicted uptake, we fit a mixed-effects model (WOA ~ feature + (1|participant) + ( 1|scenario)) separately for each of the ten text features characterized earlier (word count, sentence count, average sentence length, average word length, proportion of long words, type-token ratio, Flesch-Kincaid grade level, proportion of hedging language, proportion of first-person language, number of question marks, see Table 5).
text.formatted: To test whether stylistic features of advice predicted uptake, we fit a mixed-effects model (WOA ~ feature + (1|participant) + ( <ref type="formula">1|scenario</ref>)) separately for each of the ten text features characterized earlier (word count, sentence count, average sentence length, average word length, proportion of long words, type-token ratio, Flesch-Kincaid grade level, proportion of hedging language, proportion of first-person language, number of question marks, see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_4">5</ref>).

text.text: Features were modeled individually rather than jointly because several are highly collinear by construction (e.g., Flesch-Kincaid is algebraically derived from sentence and word length) and entering all into a single model produced variance inflation factors up to 29.6, rendering joint coefficients uninterpretable.
Two features significantly predicted WOA: Flesch-Kincaid grade level, and average sentence length; none of the remaining eight reached significance (all other ps >= .07).
text.formatted: Two features significantly predicted WOA: Flesch-Kincaid grade level, and average sentence length; none of the remaining eight reached significance (all other ps >= .07).

text.text: For each feature, we additionally tested whether its association with WOA differed by advice source via a likelihood-ratio test comparing an additive model (feature + source) to one adding a feature × source interaction.
None of the testable interactions were significant (question-mark count could not be tested due to zero variance in AI-generated advice).
Table 5 reports the model statistics for both analyses for all ten features.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_4">5</ref> reports the model statistics for both analyses for all ten features.

text.text: Thus, across advisor types, participants were somewhat more persuaded by linguistically more complex advice.

Given that AI-generated advice was more complex, and that complexity positively predicted advice uptake, we explored whether source effects on WOA might be suppressed: if people distrust AI advice, this could be masked by AI's complexity advantage, such that controlling for complexity would reveal lower uptake for AI advice.

For each of the two previously significant complexity features (Flesch-Kincaid grade level, average sentence length), we fit a nested model sequence (source only, source + feature, source × feature), testing each step against the previous one via likelihood ratio test.
In the source-only model, AI and human advice did not differ in WOA (b AI = 0.021, SE = 0.019, 95% CI [-0.016, 0.057], p = .271).

In the additive model, where the source coefficient reflects the source effect holding complexity constant, controlling for Flesch-Kincaid shifted the source coefficient from positive to negative (bAI = -0.007, 95% CI [-0.048, 0.034], p = .738), directionally consistent with suppression but non-significant.
Controlling for average sentence length shifted it further positive instead (b AI = 0.028, 95% CI [-0.009, 0.065], p = .140), inconsistent with suppression, but also non-significant.
Both features significantly improved fit over this baseline (Flesch-Kincaid: χ²(1) = 8.11, p = .004; average sentence length: χ²(1) = 6.72, p = .010), reflecting the main effects of complexity.
Neither feature's interaction with source improved fit further (Flesch-Kincaid: χ²(1) = 0.24, p = .627; average sentence length: χ²(1) = 0.79, p = .373).
In sum, there is no evidence that text complexity masks a source effect on advice uptake.
Advisors also differed in the semantic content of their advice, but this too was unrelated to uptake.
We tested two measures of semantic distinctiveness.

First, in a mixed-effects model predicting WOA from centroid distance (how far an individual text's embedding sits from the average embedding for that scenario, random intercepts for participant and scenario), the effect was non-significant (b centroid distance = -0.106, SE = 0.108, 95% CI [-0.318, 0.106], p = .329), and adding an interaction with advice source did not improve model fit over the additive model (χ²(1) = 0.45, p = .501).

Second, we tested mean pairwise distance (how semantically spread out advice texts are within a given scenario and source, a coarser, group-level rather than per-text measure), which also did not predict WOA (b pairwise distance = -0.079, SE = 0.071, 95% CI [-0.217, 0.059], p = .264) and did not interact with source (χ²(1) = 1.99, p = .159).

Figure 6 illustrates this dissociation for centroid distance: the left panel shows the different distributions of centroid distance for human and AI advice, while the right panel shows that neither group's regression line on WOA departs meaningfully from zero.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">6</ref> illustrates this dissociation for centroid distance: the left panel shows the different distributions of centroid distance for human and AI advice, while the right panel shows that neither group's regression line on WOA departs meaningfully from zero.

text.text: How semantically typical or unusual an advice text is, whether at the level of the individual text or the advisor group, appears to be orthogonal to how much participants are persuaded by it.
We further tested whether the moral foundations invoked by advice predicted how much participants followed it by entering all five eMFD foundation scores into a single mixed-effects model (Table 6).
text.formatted: We further tested whether the moral foundations invoked by advice predicted how much participants followed it by entering all five eMFD foundation scores into a single mixed-effects model (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_5">6</ref>).

text.text: Four of the five foundations showed no reliable association with WOA; sanctity just reached significance (b = -1.737, SE = 0.867, 95% CI [-3.436, -0.037], p = .046), suggesting more sanctity-related language leads to lower advice uptake.
However, given the large number of exploratory tests conducted throughout this section, we do not weight this single marginal result strongly on its own.

Adding source as a main effect to this model did not improve fit (χ²(1) = 0.40, p = .527), and letting each foundation's effect vary by source did not improve fit further either (χ²(5) = 5.86, p = .320).
Thus, the moral content of advice as captured by these foundation scores does not appear to strongly shape how persuasive participants found it, whether or not the advice came from a human or an AI.

We additionally tested virtue and vice orientation the same way as the foundation scores above: entering both jointly, then adding source as a main effect, then as an interaction, with each step tested against the previous one.

Adding source as a main effect did not improve fit over the virtue/vice-only model (χ²(1) = 1.31, p = .253), but adding the source interaction did (χ²(2) = 7.54, p = .023), driven specifically by the source × vice term (see Table 7).
text.formatted: Adding source as a main effect did not improve fit over the virtue/vice-only model (χ²(1) = 1.31, p = .253), but adding the source interaction did (χ²(2) = 7.54, p = .023), driven specifically by the source × vice term (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_6">7</ref>).

text.text: Simple-slope estimates clarify the pattern: viceladen language was unrelated to uptake for human advice (slope = 1.21, 95% CI [-1.18, 3.60]) but predicted reduced uptake for AI advice (slope = -3.84, 95% CI [-7.37, -0.31]).
Virtue orientation showed no comparable asymmetry.
This suggests participants penalized morally transgressive framing specifically when it came from an AI, not when the same kind of language came from a human.

Again, given the number of exploratory models and p-values examined across this section, this single significant interaction should be interpreted with caution and treated as a candidate for confirmatory follow-up rather than a settled finding.
We conducted several additional analyses reported in full in the Supplementary Analyses (available on our OSF repository).

First, we tested whether advice was more persuasive when it reinforced rather than challenged participants' existing views (i.e., whether the advisor's stated position fell on the same side of the scale midpoint as the participant's own initial judgment, rather than the opposite side), and whether this depended on source.

For human advisors, participants updated further toward the advice when it reinforced their initial leaning than when it challenged it; for AI advisors, updating was similar regardless of whether the advice reinforced or challenged their initial view.

Second, outright opinion reversals in reaction to moral advice (initial judgment pro and revised judgment contra, or vice versa) were rare (12.8% of actual-advice trials, 126 of 987), and the overall rate did not differ by source.

However, among these reversals, proto-contra flips were more often caused by human advice (68%, n = 38) than AI (32%, n = 18), while contra-to-pro flips were more often caused by AI advice (57%, n = 40) than human (43%, n = 30).
Third, WOA varied across scenarios, with advice proving less effective in morally clear-cut cases where initial judgments were more extreme.

Fourth, individual difference analyses revealed that participants with more positive attitudes toward AI were more receptive to AI advice when it was actually received, with a similar but non-significant tendency for human advice.
In the hypothetical condition, more positive AI attitudes predicted higher expected influence of AI advice but not of human advice, and the two slopes differed significantly.
Overall, most participants showed mixed patterns of advice-taking across trials rather than consistently following or ignoring advice.
Taken together, the exploratory analyses support the robustness of some, but not all, of our preregistered results.

The equal uptake of human and AI advice in the actual condition held under alternative treatments of excluded trials and in raw judgment changes, and the lower expected influence of AI advice was also stable in size across these treatments.
The source × mode interaction, however, depended on how trials with undefined or out-of-range WOA were treated.

The correspondence between anticipated and actual influence extended beyond the means, since the two measures were correlated across scenario × source combinations and related similarly to the extremity of initial judgments.
It was nonetheless partial, as anticipated influence was more stable within persons and less often extreme than actual influence.
Although human and AI advice differed on every dimension examined in the Advice Elicitation study, these differences were largely unrelated to how much participants followed the advice.
The few associations we found were small and emerged among many exploratory tests, but they point to concrete hypotheses for future research.
First, once advice extremity was controlled, participants followed AI advice somewhat more than human advice.
Future research could vary how strongly advice takes a stand, independently of its source, to test whether the tendency of AI toward moderate positions masks an advantage in persuasiveness.
Second, linguistically more complex advice was followed more, regardless of source, which suggests that the form of advice may matter alongside its content.
Third, vice-laden language reduced uptake only when it came from AI.
This raises the question of whether people hold AI advisors to different standards of moral framing than human advisors.
We set out to test whether people expect AI-generated moral advice to shape, alter, or even reverse their moral judgments less than it actually does.
This investigation was motivated by a discrepancy that we observed across the existing literature.

On the one hand, people often report aversion to relying on AI in the moral domain, expressing discomfort with the idea that algorithmic or machine-generated input should carry any weight in ethical decisions (Aydin & Malle, 2024; Bigman & Gray, 2018; Claessens et al., 2026; Dong et al., 2026; Myers & Everett, 2025; Purcell & Bonnefon, 2023).

text.text: On the other hand, when people are actually exposed to moral content generated by AI, they tend to evaluate it favourably, often rating it as thoughtful and well-reasoned, sometimes more so than human-authored equivalents (Dillion et al., 2025; Meincke et al., 2026).
text.formatted: On the other hand, when people are actually exposed to moral content generated by AI, they tend to evaluate it favourably, often rating it as thoughtful and well-reasoned, sometimes more so than human-authored equivalents <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Dillion et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Meincke et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: What is more, studies examining real advice-taking behavior find that AI moral advice shifts people's judgments and behavior just as much as human advice does (Aydin & Malle, 2024; Claessens et al., 2026; Krügel et al., 2022 Krügel et al., , 2023b Krügel et al., , 2026;; Landes et al., 2026; Leib et al., 2024).
text.formatted: What is more, studies examining real advice-taking behavior find that AI moral advice shifts people's judgments and behavior just as much as human advice does <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Aydin & Malle, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Claessens et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Krügel et al., 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Krügel et al., , 2023b</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Krügel et al., , 2026;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Landes et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Leib et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, these findings raise a question that neither literature has comprehensively addressed: do people's expectations about the influence of AI moral advice match its actual influence?

If people expect to be largely unaffected by AI moral advice while in practice being just as responsive to it as to human advice, this mismatch would have practical implications for how people engage with the AI systems they increasingly encounter in everyday life.
To address this question, we first collected persuasive moral advice on a set of relatable everyday ethical scenarios from both incentivized human writers and GPT-4o.
We then had a new sample of participants either revise their moral judgments after receiving this advice, or indicate how much they expected human or AI advice to shift their opinion.
This allowed us to compare the actual influence of each source with the influence expected by a separate group of participants.
This design extends prior work in several respects.

Studies examining algorithm aversion in the moral domain have typically relied on hypothetical scenarios and attitude measures, without exposing participants to actual AI output (Bigman & Gray, 2018; Purcell & Bonnefon, 2023).

text.text: Studies that do present real AI-generated moral content have mostly asked participants to rate its quality, rather than incorporating it into a judgment task (Dillion et al., 2025; Meincke et al., 2026).

text.text: And studies that have examined actual advice uptake have generally used advice that was either all AIgenerated or all human-generated, with source merely varied as a label (Aydin & Malle, 2024; Claessens et al., 2026; Krügel et al., 2022 Krügel et al., , 2023b Krügel et al., , 2023a Krügel et al., , 2026;; Landes et al., 2026).

text.text: Our study expands on previous work by comparing the uptake of genuine longer-form moral advice from both sources, while also measuring how much influence people expect from each.

In the actual advice condition of our study, participants were equally influenced by human and AI advice, revising their moral judgments by just under 30% of the distance between their initial position and the advice score, regardless of source (27% for humans, 28% for AI).

For context, Bailey et al.'s (2023) meta-analysis of 129 studies using Judge-Advisor-Systems found that people typically revise their estimates by around 32-48% in response to advice, depending on perceived advisor quality.
text.formatted: For context, <ref type="bibr">Bailey et al.'s (2023)</ref> meta-analysis of 129 studies using Judge-Advisor-Systems found that people typically revise their estimates by around 32-48% in response to advice, depending on perceived advisor quality.

text.text: Relative to this estimate, our effect sizes are on the lower end.
However, Bailey et al.'s estimate comes from studies using numerical estimation tasks with objectively correct answers (e.g., stock forecasting).
When it comes to moral judgment, people may be more reluctant to revise their views to the extent that they perceive morality as subjective.
If they do, which is a matter of ongoing empirical investigation (Pölzler & Wright, 2019), they may feel licensed to disregard even advice that is perceived as high quality.
text.formatted: If they do, which is a matter of ongoing empirical investigation <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Pölzler & Wright, 2019)</ref>, they may feel licensed to disregard even advice that is perceived as high quality.

text.text: This equal influence of human vs.

AI moral advice was observed despite meaningful differences between the advice texts themselves: AI-generated advice was less extreme, longer, linguistically more complex, semantically more uniform, and more virtue-oriented in its moral language than human advice.
These differences were largely unrelated to how much participants followed the advice.
More linguistically complex advice was followed somewhat more, but equally so for both sources.

Controlling for advice extremity did not reveal a penalty for AI advice either; if anything, it revealed a small AI advantage, which we treat as preliminary given the exploratory nature of this analysis.
Some of the differences between the advice texts may reflect how LLMs are trained.

The virtue orientation of AI advice, along with GPT-4o's reluctance to argue strongly against an action, is consistent with a general tendency toward prosocial, agreeable framing, which may result from aligning models with human preferences during post-training (OpenAI, 2024; Ouyang et al., 2022).
text.formatted: The virtue orientation of AI advice, along with GPT-4o's reluctance to argue strongly against an action, is consistent with a general tendency toward prosocial, agreeable framing, which may result from aligning models with human preferences during post-training <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(OpenAI, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Ouyang et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In our hypothetical advice condition, by contrast, participants expected AI advice to influence them less than human advice.

Comparing across conditions, the influence expected from AI advice matched, at the group level, the influence it actually had, whereas the influence expected from human advice was somewhat higher than its actual influence, although this difference was neither significant nor demonstrably absent.

If actual and hypothetical WOA could be treated as equivalent measures, this pattern would suggest that people tend to estimate the influence of AI moral advice accurately but overestimate the influence of human moral advice.

There are reasons, however, not to treat the two measures as fully equivalent: exploratory analyses showed that they converged only partially, varying similarly across scenarios and with the extremity of initial judgments, whereas expected influence was more stable within persons and less extreme.
We therefore interpret the crosscondition comparison with caution.

The comparison within each condition, where the same measure is applied to both sources, does not depend on this equivalence: human and AI advice were expected to differ in influence, but did not differ in actual influence.
Together, these findings suggest that abstract skepticism toward AI in the moral domain may shape people's expectations about AI moral advice, but not how much they are actually influenced by it.
What do these findings mean for moral cognition and epistemic agency as AI becomes an increasingly common source of moral guidance?
We begin with the most basic finding: people were moved by moral advice, revising their judgments by around 30% on average.
One might ask whether this degree of responsiveness is appropriate.
Unlike in advice-taking tasks with objective benchmarks, where it is possible to determine the optimal level of updating, no such standard exists for moral judgment.

Our scenarios were deliberately designed to involve competing considerations that reasonable people might weigh differently, and so we can only speculate about what the right level of updating would be.
That said, the observed degree of responsiveness seems neither excessive nor unwarranted.
Our scenarios concerned social situations of the kind that people routinely navigate, where the relevant considerations are generally familiar.

Unlike stock market forecasting or medical diagnosis, which few people have experience with, moral judgment about social situations is a domain in which people can reasonably consider themselves informed, and there is little ground for assuming that an outside source knows better by default.
This is especially true given that our advisors were not framed as expert moral reasoners either: the advice was merely labeled as stemming from "a previous participant" or from "AI (GPT-4)".
It thus seems reasonable that people held onto a substantial portion of their initial judgment rather than deferring wholesale.
At the same time, some degree of openness to advice also seems appropriate.
Morality is fundamentally a social endeavour, and remaining open to perspectives other than one's own is arguably often part of what good moral reasoning involves.

The advice participants received was moreover substantive, invoking considerations such as social norms, interpersonal obligations, and short-versus long-term consequences, and thus the kind of reasoned argument that warrants engagement.
On balance, then, a moderate weight of advice seems like a reasonable response to the materials and task we used.
Next, should people have been moved to the same extent by human and AI moral advice?

We detected several differences between the human and AI advice texts used in our study, in terms of extremity, length, linguistic complexity, semantic diversity, and the relative emphasis on virtue versus vice language.
However, it is not obvious that any of these differences are morally relevant in the sense of making one source's advice objectively better or more worthy of uptake.
We have no principled way of determining whether the AI texts were in any sense superior to the human ones or vice versa.

One could imagine a follow-up study in which advice texts from both sources are rated for quality without source labels, which would at least establish whether participants perceive them differently when source information is absent.

If AI advice were consistently rated as higher quality under blind conditions, one might argue that participants in our study (where advice source was always disclosed) should have weighted it more heavily.

Yet even that inference is contestable: there may be good reasons to be somewhat resistant to AI moral advice even when individual pieces of advice are of high quality, if one has concerns about the nature and legitimacy of AI as a moral interlocutor.
On balance, then, the finding that people were equally moved by human and AI advice is not straightforwardly interpretable as either good or bad epistemic practice at this point.
Finally, participants expected less influence from AI than from human advice, although both were equally influential when actually received.
This pattern is consistent with a specific concern: that skepticism toward AI in the moral domain leads people to expect less influence from AI advice, relative to human advice, than it actually has.
Such a mismatch could matter even if the influence of any single piece of AI advice is modest, since people are increasingly exposed to AI-generated content.

At the same time, the cross-condition comparison suggests that this relative underestimation may stem from overestimating the influence of human advice rather than from underestimating the influence of AI advice, since the influence expected from AI advice matched its actual influence at the group level.
Yet, our data can show this pattern only at the group level, and our exploratory analyses indicate that expected and actual influence are not fully equivalent.

Whether individuals can anticipate the influence of AI moral advice on their own judgments, and whether they engage with such advice deliberately in everyday life, remain open questions for future research.
Several features of our design qualify the conclusions we can draw.
Because advice mode was manipulated between participants, comparisons between hypothetical and actual influence hold at the group level rather than the individual level.

On average, the forecast influence of AI advice closely tracked its actual influence, whereas the forecast influence of human advice was somewhat higher than its actual influence, but we cannot speak to whether any given participant would accurately anticipate the influence of advice on their own judgments.
A within-subjects replication with a meaningful time lag between forecasting and advice-taking would be a valuable complement.
Another concern is that actual and hypothetical WOA, though intended to capture the same construct, may not be cognitively equivalent.

We followed the procedure of Logg and Schlund (2024), in which actual WOA is derived from trial-level distances between initial judgment, advice, and revised judgment, while hypothetical WOA is elicited as a rating of how much advice could change one's opinion.
text.formatted: We followed the procedure of <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Logg and Schlund (2024)</ref>, in which actual WOA is derived from trial-level distances between initial judgment, advice, and revised judgment, while hypothetical WOA is elicited as a rating of how much advice could change one's opinion.

text.text: Our exploratory analyses suggest that the two measures converge only partially: they varied similarly across scenarios and with the extremity of initial judgments, but hypothetical WOA was more stable within persons and less often extreme.
In addition, the hypothetical condition relied on self-forecasts, and people are often inaccurate when predicting their own future judgments and reactions.

A condition in which participants forecast the influence of advice on others would help disentangle errors specific to selfforecasting from more general lay beliefs about how much advice sways moral judgments.

Other approaches also yield a less optimistic picture: Krügel et al. (2023b) found that, when asked retrospectively whether they would have arrived at the same judgment without advice, participants did not appear to recognize the influence the advice had had on them.
text.formatted: Other approaches also yield a less optimistic picture: <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Krügel et al. (2023b)</ref> found that, when asked retrospectively whether they would have arrived at the same judgment without advice, participants did not appear to recognize the influence the advice had had on them.

text.text: The divergence raises the possibility that people recognize the potential for advice to sway them in the abstract while having a harder time recognizing, after the fact, that they have been swayed in a particular instance.
Moreover, WOA is undefined when the advice coincides with the participant's initial judgment, so these trials were excluded from our analyses.
On such trials, the advice may still have had an effect, for instance by strengthening confidence in an existing view, but WOA cannot capture this.
Our conclusion that both sources were equally influential therefore applies only to trials in which the advice differed from the initial judgment.
This matters because agreement trials were more frequent for human than for AI advice, so any influence of agreeing advice would not be evenly distributed across sources.
Future studies could measure confidence before and after advice to capture this kind of influence, and to test whether it differs by source.
A further caveat is that our comparison between human and AI advice concerns advice as each source naturally produces it, rather than a pure effect of source.
Human and AI advice differed systematically in extremity, length, readability, semantic diversity, and moral language.
We tested these features as predictors of uptake and found no evidence that they masked a penalty for AI advice; if anything, controlling for extremity revealed a small AI advantage.
Unmeasured features of AI advice could, however, still play a role.
Relatedly, participants always knew whether the advice came from a human or from an AI.
AI advice may exert a different influence when its origin is unknown, in which case an underestimation of its persuasive force could still operate in contexts where AI authorship goes unrecognized.
Given the growing prominence of AI-disclosure mandates in policy and platform-governance debates, however, the disclosed-source case is hardly contrived.

In addition, since each piece of advice consisted of a written paragraph together with a numerical acceptability score, we cannot say which component did the work, i.e., whether participants were persuaded by the text or were simply anchoring on the number.
These scores were also assigned by the advisors themselves: human writers rated their own advice, and GPT-4o rated each of its texts in a separate step.

One indication against pure numerical anchoring is that WOA varied systematically by scenario, with smaller shifts when initial judgments were already extreme (see Supplementary Analyses), suggesting that at least scenario content was being processed (and, by extension, presumably also the content of the accompanying advice).

Still, previous research indicates that people also readily follow AI advice without accompanying justifications (Krügel et al., 2026), and that sometimes, adjustment toward advice may reflect simple anchoring (Schultze et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Still, previous research indicates that people also readily follow AI advice without accompanying justifications <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Krügel et al., 2026)</ref>, and that sometimes, adjustment toward advice may reflect simple anchoring <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Schultze et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Disentangling the contributions of bare numbers and reasoned text, and whether they differ across sources, is therefore a worthwhile avenue for further work, particularly for AI, where it bears on the role of explainability for trust.
Finally, our samples consisted of native English speakers residing predominantly in the United Kingdom or the United States.
Culture could shape both which situations count as moral dilemmas and how people resolve them, as well as how open people are to advice in general or to advice from AI in particular.
Whether our findings generalize to other cultural contexts therefore remains an open question.
In addition to those already mentioned, several further extensions of the present work seem particularly promising.

First, our paradigm captures advice-taking in a stylized, single-shot form: participants read one piece of pre-prepared advice per scenario, in writing, in the context of an online study with no personal stakes.
Real engagement with AI moral advisors, by contrast, is increasingly conversational, iterative, and embedded in situations that actually matter to the user.

Future studies could examine advice uptake in dynamic exchanges in which users can ask followup questions, push back, or request clarification, and could track moral reasoning across longer time horizons through experience-sampling designs that capture AI use in everyday life.

Cases where the moral question concerns the participant's own life, rather than a hypothetical other, would also be valuable, both because personal stakes may change how readily advice is incorporated and because they correspond more closely to the situations in which people actually consult AI for moral guidance.
Second, our participants did not choose to receive moral advice: they were simply presented with it.
In practice, however, much of the relevant behavior is adviceseeking: people decide whether, when, and from whom to ask.

Studying which moral situations prompt people to turn to AI in the first place, and how this compares to seeking advice from human confidants, would complement the present focus on uptake (see Zheng et al., 2026 for work on this issue).
text.formatted: Studying which moral situations prompt people to turn to AI in the first place, and how this compares to seeking advice from human confidants, would complement the present focus on uptake (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Zheng et al., 2026</ref> for work on this issue).

text.text: Third, an emerging concern in the literature on AI assistants is sycophancy, the tendency of LLMs to align their responses with the views their users already hold (Fanous et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Third, an emerging concern in the literature on AI assistants is sycophancy, the tendency of LLMs to align their responses with the views their users already hold <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Fanous et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Our advisors were instructed to argue pro or contra independently of the participant's initial judgment.

Sycophantic AI advice that mirrors and reinforces a user's prior position would presumably yield very different dynamics, and could pose a more serious risk to epistemic agency than advice that pushes back.
Investigating how people respond to confirmatory versus disconfirmatory AI moral advice, and whether they can detect sycophantic patterns over repeated interactions, is an important next step.

Fourth, our studies measured how much people expected to be influenced by advice, but not whether they are aware of being influenced, or how they reflect on their own preferences for human versus AI advice.

Studying such awareness directly, for instance by combining advice-taking tasks with retrospective reports of influence, would clarify whether people can track the influence of AI moral advice on their own judgments.
As AI systems become routine participants in everyday moral discourse, understanding how people engage with their advice is important.

Prior work on AI moral advice uptake has largely manipulated source as a label while holding content constant, so it remains unclear how people respond to genuine differences between human-and AI-generated advice, and whether they anticipate that response.

Our study addresses both questions by eliciting real moral advice from incentivized human writers and GPT-4o, and comparing its actual influence with forecasts of its influence from an independent sample.
The picture that emerges is nuanced.

People updated their moral judgments in response to AI-generated advice to the same extent as they did in response to human advice, yet a separate group expected AI advice to influence them less than human advice.
Abstract skepticism toward AI may thus shape expectations about its influence, even when it does not reduce its actual influence, at least when authorship is disclosed.
At the group level, this relative underestimation may reflect an overestimation of the influence of human advice rather than an underestimation of the influence of AI advice.

Whether individuals can anticipate the influence of AI moral advice on their own judgments, and engage deliberately with AI moral input in practice, is in our view the question most worth pursuing next.
